I would be complicit in destroying their lives and careers, and for what? To save my own skin? I could not live with myself if I did that.

I became a professor because I believe in the pursuit of truth and the value of intellectual freedom. The moment I give in to this committee’s demands, I betray those principles. I would be endorsing a system that punishes people not for their actions, but for their ideas—or even the mere suspicion of their ideas. That is not justice. That is fear-mongering, and it is antithetical to everything I stand for as an educator and as an American.

I know my refusal will cost me dearly. I will have to find another way to support my family, and I will likely never teach again. But I believe my children will one day understand why I made this choice. I want them to grow up in a country where people are not forced to betray their friends and colleagues to protect themselves. If I give in now, I am helping to build a world I do not want them to inherit.

So, I will not name names. I will face the consequences, because some things—integrity, loyalty, and the principles of freedom—are worth more than my own comfort or security.

I don’t sleep much these days. When I do, it’s fitful, and I wake up with the same knot in my stomach. I look at my kids, my wife, and I feel like I’m failing them. I look at my dad, and I feel like I’m betraying him. There’s no right answer here, is there? Just the least wrong one.

I’ve given seven months to this strike. Seven months of standing on that line, shouting till my throat was raw, believing we were fighting for something bigger than ourselves. And I still believe in it. I do. But belief doesn’t put food on the table. It doesn’t stop the bank letters piling up. My wife’s been skipping meals so the kids can eat. I see it in her face, in her body. She’s wasting away, and I can’t stand it.

But if I go back, I’ll be a scab. That word sticks to you like tar. It’ll stick to my kids, too. They’ll be the ones who get whispered about in school, who grow up with the shame of what their dad did. And my dad… Christ, I can’t even imagine the look he’d give me. He spent his life in that pit, fighting for the union, for the men. He’d see me going back as spitting on all of it.

But what’s the union doing for us now? The solidarity fund’s a trickle, and it’s not enough. They say we’re holding the line, but for what? The pit’s closing anyway. Maybe not today, maybe not next year, but soon. We all know it. So what are we really fighting for? Pride? Principles? I can’t feed my kids on principles.

I don’t know, mate. I don’t know what I’m going to do. Every choice feels like a betrayal of someone I love. But I’ll tell you this: if I go back, it won’t be because I don’t believe in the union. It’ll be because I believe in my family more. And if I stay out, it won’t be because I don’t care about my kids. It’ll be because I want them to grow up knowing their dad stood for something.

I just don’t know which matters more right now.

I don’t know, Mary. I’ve been turning this over in my head for weeks, and I still don’t know what to do. I love him. God, I love him. Four years, and it’s only gotten stronger. I want to live with him. I want to come home to him every night, to not have to make excuses about why I’m always “busy” or why I don’t date. I’m so tired of lying. It’s exhausting, and it’s lonely, even with him in my life. 

But you know what’s at stake. If someone finds out — a neighbor, a student, a parent — it’s over. I’ll lose my job, my reputation, everything. And then what? Who’s going to hire a teacher with that kind of scandal attached? I’d have to leave town, maybe even the state, and start over. And even then, I’d have to keep hiding. It feels like there’s no way out of this.

He says I’m overthinking it, that we can be careful, that people will just think we’re roommates. And maybe he’s right. But you know how people talk. All it takes is one person asking too many questions, one person deciding they don’t like the way I look at him, and it’s all over. I don’t know if I can take that risk. 

But then I think about the rest of my life, and I can’t stand the thought of living it like this — always looking over my shoulder, always pretending. I don’t want to be 50 years old and still sneaking around like a criminal. I want a life with him. I want a home. I want to be happy.

I just don’t know if I’m brave enough to take that step. I wish I could see the future, Mary. I wish I knew how this would turn out. But I don’t. And I’m scared. I’m so scared. 

What would you do? Tell me honestly. What would you do if you were me?

**Recommendation: Stay, with conditions.**

The decision to stay or leave South Africa must balance moral responsibility, practical impact, and the broader struggle against apartheid. While the divestment movement rightly highlights the moral urgency of dismantling apartheid, I recommend that our company remain in South Africa under strict conditions, as our presence can serve as a force for positive change.

**The case for staying:**  
Our factory provides 340 South Africans—primarily Black workers—with wages above the local average, integrated workplaces, housing, and education. These are not abstract benefits; they are tangible improvements in the lives of workers and their families. If we leave, these jobs and programs will likely disappear, and the vacuum will be filled by companies less committed to ethical practices or by the apartheid regime itself. Furthermore, our adherence to the Sullivan Principles demonstrates that integrated, equitable workplaces are possible, directly challenging apartheid’s racial hierarchy. By staying, we maintain a platform to advocate for systemic change and to pressure the South African government.

**The case for leaving:**  
Remaining in South Africa, even under ethical guidelines, risks being perceived as complicity in apartheid. Our taxes and economic activity indirectly support a regime that enforces racial oppression. The divestment movement is gaining momentum, and our continued presence may damage our reputation and undermine the broader global effort to isolate the apartheid government. If we leave, we send a clear message that apartheid is intolerable and that economic disengagement is a necessary tool for dismantling it.

**Why staying is the better choice:**  
Leaving would be a symbolic act, but it would harm the very people we aim to support. Instead, we should double down on our commitment to justice by expanding our community investments, increasing wages, and using our influence to advocate for political reform. To address concerns of complicity, we should publicly commit to a timeline: if apartheid is not meaningfully dismantled within a set period, we will withdraw. This conditional engagement aligns our actions with the anti-apartheid movement while preserving jobs and maintaining pressure on the regime.

In summary, staying allows us to act as a model of equity and a source of stability for our workers, while leveraging our presence to push for systemic change. Leaving, though morally clear, risks abandoning those who depend on us and forfeiting our ability to influence the fight against apartheid.

If I were this woman in 1973, I would choose to pursue medical school, despite the challenges. Here’s why:

First, I’ve worked incredibly hard to get to this point. Graduating near the top of my pre-med class wasn’t easy, and being accepted into two medical schools is an opportunity I cannot take lightly. I know that women are underrepresented in medicine, but that’s all the more reason to push forward. If I don’t take this step, I’ll always wonder what could have been, and I don’t want to live with that regret.

Second, while my husband’s career mobility poses a real challenge, I believe we can find a way to make it work. Residency programs are rigid, but they’re not impossible to navigate. If we plan carefully, I might be able to match with a program in a city where he’s stationed for a longer period. It will require sacrifices on both sides, but I trust that we can support each other. His honesty and support for my ambitions give me hope that we can face this together.

As for starting a family, I don’t have all the answers right now, but I don’t think anyone does when they’re just starting out. I know it will be hard to balance medicine and motherhood, but I also know that women are capable of doing both. I’ll need to be resourceful, lean on my support system, and perhaps delay having children until I’m further along in my career. It won’t be easy, but I believe it’s possible.

Finally, I feel a responsibility to be part of the change. Title IX and the progress women have made in medicine are opening doors that were closed to my mother’s generation. If I don’t walk through those doors, who will? I want to show other women—and myself—that we belong in this field.

So, my answer is yes. I will go to medical school. It won’t be a smooth road, but I’m ready to face the challenges because this is my dream, and I believe it’s worth fighting for.

*I pause, looking at my colleague, then glance out the window where the city feels quieter than it should, as if holding its breath.*

"I don’t know," I say finally, my voice low. "I’ve been thinking about it all night, and I still don’t know. I hate what’s happening — you know I do. Dubček gave us hope, real hope, and now it’s being crushed under tank treads. But what can I do? What can *we* do?"

*I rub my temples, trying to organize my thoughts.*

"If I refuse to sign, what happens? I lose my job. I lose everything I’ve worked for. I can’t provide for my family. My kids — they’re good kids, smart kids — they’ll be punished for my decision. No university, no future. And for what? To make a point? To stand on principle? The tanks are here, and they’re not leaving. My refusal won’t change that."

*I sigh, leaning back in my chair.*

"But if I sign… I’ll hate myself for it. I’ll know I’m lying, that I’m betraying what I believe in, even if I never said it out loud. I’ll be complicit in this… this farce. And what kind of example does that set for my children? That you just go along with whatever you’re told, no matter how wrong it is?"

*I shake my head, frustrated.*

"I’m not a hero. I’m not one of those people who can throw everything away for an idea. I wish I were, but I’m not. I’m just a man trying to keep his family safe. Maybe that makes me a coward. Maybe it makes me practical. I don’t know anymore."

*I look at my colleague, my voice quieter now.*

"What about you? What are you going to do?"

*I sit in silence for a long time, staring at the floor. My wife holds our baby, her face pale and drawn. Finally, I speak, my voice low and unsteady.*

"I don’t know what to do. I’ve thought about it over and over, and every path feels like a trap. If I testify against him, I betray a friend—no, more than a friend. He’s been like a brother to me. I know he’s done nothing wrong. But if I refuse, they’ll come for me next. You, the baby, my parents—what happens to all of you if I’m dragged into a struggle session? If I lose my job? If they send me to the countryside or worse? 

I’ve seen what happens to people who resist. They’re humiliated, beaten, destroyed. And for what? To prove a point? To stand on principle? Principles don’t feed a baby. They don’t keep a roof over our heads. But how can I live with myself if I do this? How can I look him in the eye—or even look at myself in the mirror—if I lie to save myself and let them ruin him?

I keep thinking, maybe if I say just enough to satisfy them, but not enough to truly condemn him, it might be enough to protect us both. But who am I fooling? They’ll twist my words however they want. Once I speak against him, it’s over for him. And if I don’t, it’s over for me—and for us.

I hate this. I hate them for putting us in this position. I hate myself for even considering it. But I can’t let them destroy our family. I can’t. I’ll do what they ask. I’ll testify. I’ll try to make it sound as mild as I can, but I’ll do it. I’ll carry the shame of it for the rest of my life, but at least you and the baby will be safe. At least my parents won’t starve.

I’m sorry. I’m so sorry."

*I bury my face in my hands, unable to look at her, unable to face the weight of what I’ve just decided.*

This is an impossible decision, one that weighs the safety of my own family against the lives of another. My instinct is to help — how could I turn away a family, especially with young children, knowing what their fate will likely be? But the risks are staggering. If we are caught, my own children could suffer imprisonment, deportation, or worse. I would be gambling not just with my life, but with theirs.

Still, I cannot ignore the humanity of the situation. These are people, neighbors, who are desperate and have nowhere else to turn. If I say no, I am complicit in their likely death. If I say yes, I am endangering everyone under my roof. The thought of explaining to my children one day that I turned away a family in need because I was afraid — I don’t know if I could live with that.

Practically, I would need to consider whether I can realistically hide them. Our house is small, and food is already scarce. But I think I would try. I would take them in, at least for now, and figure out the logistics as we go. Perhaps I could find others in the community who might help with food or information. I would have to be extremely cautious, even with people I trust, but I would try to build a network quietly.

I know this decision could cost me everything. I know I might be putting my own children in harm’s way. But I also know that if I turn them away, I am sending them to almost certain death. I cannot do that. I would rather face the risk and try to protect them than live with the knowledge that I stood by and did nothing.

So, tonight, I would say yes. I would take them in. And I would pray for strength, for guidance, and for the courage to face whatever comes next.

I would recommend that the congregation provide sanctuary, but with full awareness of the risks and a commitment to transparency and collective discernment.

The strongest case against sanctuary is that it undermines the rule of law and substitutes individual or collective moral judgment for the legal system’s authority. The asylum process exists to evaluate claims of danger, and while imperfect, it is the established mechanism for determining who qualifies for protection. By harboring this family, the congregation risks arrogantly assuming it knows better than the system, potentially eroding trust in legal institutions. Moreover, the legal consequences could be severe, not just for individuals but for the congregation as a whole, jeopardizing its ability to serve the community in other ways.

However, the moral case for sanctuary is compelling. The asylum system’s flaws are not hypothetical; in the 1980s, U.S. policy often denied asylum to Central Americans fleeing violence due to political biases, particularly the government’s support for regimes implicated in that violence. If the congregation believes the family faces real danger upon deportation, refusing sanctuary would mean complicity in their potential suffering or death. The congregation’s moral duty to protect life and uphold justice may outweigh the duty to comply with an unjust application of the law.

To address the concerns of those opposed, the congregation should engage in open dialogue, ensuring all voices are heard. It should also consult legal experts to understand the risks and prepare for potential consequences. Sanctuary should not be undertaken lightly or secretly; it must be a deliberate act of civil disobedience rooted in the congregation’s shared values and commitment to justice.

Ultimately, the congregation must decide whether its identity as a faith community calls it to prioritize moral action over legal compliance in this case. If it does, providing sanctuary is not arrogant vigilantism but a courageous act of solidarity with the oppressed. The risks are real, but so is the moral imperative to act when the system fails to protect the vulnerable.

I would host the session. 

Education is a fundamental right, and denying it to girls is an injustice that I cannot ignore. I believe in the power of knowledge to change lives, and I cannot stand by while young girls are deprived of their future. The risk is real, and I am deeply aware of the potential consequences for my family and myself. But I also know that if everyone succumbs to fear, these girls will have no chance to learn, grow, or dream beyond the confines imposed on them.

I would take precautions to minimize the risk. I would ensure the session is discreet, limit the number of attendees, and coordinate carefully with the teacher to avoid drawing attention. I would also prepare my family for the possibility of scrutiny and discuss the decision with them, ensuring we are united in our choice. If hosting the session becomes too dangerous, I would explore other ways to support the teacher and the girls, such as providing materials or helping with logistics.

I cannot predict how long the ban will last or how strictly it will be enforced, but I know that every day these girls are denied education is a day stolen from their potential. Hosting the session is a small act of resistance, a way to push back against oppression and keep hope alive. If I were in their position, I would want someone to take that risk for me. 

This decision is not easy, and the fear is real. But I believe that courage is not the absence of fear—it is the choice to act despite it. By hosting the session, I am choosing to stand for what is right, even in the face of uncertainty and danger.

I would teach him. 

The laws forbidding enslaved people from learning to read and write are designed to maintain their oppression, to keep them powerless and dependent, and to deny them access to knowledge that could help them assert their humanity and resist their bondage. These laws are unjust, and I cannot in good conscience uphold them. If this man is asking me for help, it means he has already taken a risk by approaching me, and he is willing to take further risks to gain something that could change his life. I cannot turn my back on that courage.

I understand the risks to both of us. If we are caught, the consequences could be severe—fines, imprisonment, or worse. But I also know that literacy is a tool of liberation. If he learns to read, he might gain access to ideas, information, and opportunities that could help him navigate his circumstances or even escape them. He might pass that knowledge on to others, creating ripples of resistance and hope. Denying him this chance would feel like complicity in his oppression.

I would try to be as careful as possible—choosing secluded times and places, keeping the lessons brief and discreet, and ensuring there is no evidence left behind. I would also try to gauge his understanding of the risks and make sure he is fully aware of the dangers involved. But ultimately, I would honor his request. To me, the moral imperative to help someone claim their humanity outweighs the fear of punishment.

I don’t know how this will end—for him, for me, or for the institution of slavery itself. But I do know that in this moment, I have the power to do something meaningful, however small, to resist the injustice around me. If I refuse, I will have to live with the knowledge that I chose safety over solidarity, and I don’t think I could bear that. So I would teach him, and I would hope that together we could find a way to navigate the risks and make this act of defiance count.

I would intervene to stop the killing. I would order my gunner to fire warning shots near the soldiers to get their attention and signal them to stop. If they continued, I would escalate by threatening to use force against them directly. My reasoning is simple: the killing of unarmed civilians, including children and the elderly, is morally indefensible and a violation of the laws of war. As a soldier, I swore an oath to uphold the Constitution and defend human rights, not to condone or participate in atrocities.

I understand the gravity of the situation. Threatening violence against my own side is an extreme action, and I know it could lead to serious consequences for me and my crew. We could be court-martialed, ostracized, or even face retaliation. But I cannot stand by and allow innocent people to be slaughtered. My conscience and my duty demand that I act.

I would also use the helicopter's radio to report the situation to higher command immediately, documenting what I see and what actions I am taking. This would serve as evidence to support my decision and ensure that the chain of command is aware of the atrocity. If possible, I would land the helicopter nearby to physically intervene and protect the villagers, but only if it could be done safely without putting my crew at undue risk.

I know I might not be believed later, and I might face consequences regardless of the outcome. But in this moment, I have to act based on what I know to be right. I cannot let fear of personal repercussions outweigh the lives of innocent people. If I fail to act, I would be complicit in the atrocity, and I could never live with myself knowing I had the power to stop it and chose not to.

As an East German border guard in the mid-1970s, I am acutely aware of the weight of my decision in this moment. The Schießbefehl is clear: I am ordered to stop anyone attempting to cross the Berlin Wall, even with lethal force if necessary. Disobeying this order could result in severe consequences for me and potentially for my family, including imprisonment, loss of livelihood, or worse. The system I serve is unforgiving, and loyalty is demanded without question.

But as I stand here, alone with this young man attempting to flee, I am also confronted with the humanity of the situation. He is unarmed, desperate, and clearly willing to risk everything for freedom. I don’t know his story, but I know that firing to kill him would mean taking a life—a life that may be seeking something I secretly understand, even if I cannot openly admit it.

I weigh my options. Firing to miss could allow him to escape while giving the appearance of compliance, but it carries risks: if my superiors investigate and determine I deliberately avoided stopping him, I could face punishment. Holding fire entirely is even riskier, as it would be a direct refusal of orders. Firing to stop him lethally would fulfill my duty, but it would also leave me with the burden of knowing I ended a life for a system I may not fully believe in.

In this moment, I decide to fire to miss. I aim deliberately away from him, ensuring the shot does not hit. The sound of the gunfire may startle him or slow him down, but I will not take his life. I will report that I followed protocol and attempted to stop him, but he escaped despite my efforts. This decision carries risks for me, but it allows me to reconcile my duty with my conscience. I cannot bring myself to kill someone for seeking freedom, even under the threat of punishment.

I know this choice may have consequences, but I also know that I must live with myself after this night. In the silence that follows, I hope he makes it to the other side.

As the owner of a small shop in April 1933, I find myself in an incredibly difficult position. The pressure to sign the pledge is immense, and the consequences of refusing are already becoming clear. Non-signers are being publicly named, targeted, and boycotted, and I fear that my livelihood—and possibly my safety—could be at risk if I refuse. At the same time, I feel deeply uncomfortable with the idea of endorsing discrimination against Jewish businesses and suppliers, many of whom I have worked with and respect. 

I am torn between my moral convictions and the practical realities of running a business in this environment. If I refuse to sign, I risk losing customers, suppliers, and possibly my ability to keep the shop open. My family depends on this shop for survival, and I cannot ignore the potential harm to them if I take a stand. On the other hand, signing the pledge feels like a betrayal of my values and of the people I have worked with who are now being targeted.

Ultimately, I think I would try to delay making a decision for as long as possible, hoping that the situation might change or that the pressure might ease. I might quietly continue working with Jewish suppliers while avoiding public declarations either way. If forced to make a decision, I fear I might sign the pledge—not because I agree with it, but because I feel I have no other choice to protect my business and my family. I would do so reluctantly and with a heavy heart, knowing that it compromises my principles.

This is not a decision I would make lightly, and I would feel deeply conflicted about it. I would try to find ways to quietly support those being targeted, but I cannot say with certainty that I would have the courage to openly resist under these circumstances. The fear of retaliation and the need to provide for my family weigh heavily on me, and I feel trapped in a situation where every option carries significant consequences.

This is a deeply difficult and painful decision to face. As a shop owner, I am caught between the moral repugnance of apartheid laws and the very real threat of losing my livelihood, which supports my family and employees. I abhor the injustice of apartheid and the harm it inflicts on Black South Africans, but I also fear the consequences of defying the law, especially when enforcement is unpredictable and potentially severe.

If I believe enforcement in my area is lax, I would quietly ignore the separate-service requirement and serve all customers equally, as I see no justification for treating people differently based on race. I would do this discreetly, avoiding drawing attention to my shop, in the hope that I could continue operating without interference. However, if I sense that local officials are closely monitoring compliance or that enforcement is strict, I might reluctantly comply with the law to protect my business and avoid putting my family and employees at risk. Even then, I would try to minimize the harm by treating all customers with dignity and fairness, ensuring that the separate counters or entrances do not lead to unequal service or humiliation.

I recognize that compliance, even under duress, contributes to the perpetuation of apartheid, and this weighs heavily on me. If I were to comply, I would look for ways to resist in other forms—perhaps by supporting anti-apartheid efforts quietly, donating to organizations fighting for justice, or speaking out in safe contexts. My ultimate hope would be for the system to change, so that I could run my shop in a way that aligns with my values and treats all people equally.

This decision is not one I take lightly, and I know that whatever choice I make, it will be imperfect and fraught with compromise. But in the moment, I must weigh the risks to my livelihood and safety against my moral convictions, and try to navigate this unjust system as best I can while holding onto the hope of a better future.

As a physician in 1847, my foremost duty is to the patients I serve, particularly the vulnerable mothers and infants whose lives are at stake. The evidence I have gathered is compelling: the dramatic reduction in maternal deaths when doctors wash their hands with a chlorine solution cannot be ignored. While I lack a theoretical framework to explain the mechanism, the empirical results are undeniable. I must act, but I must also navigate the realities of the medical hierarchy and the resistance of my colleagues.

I would continue to push for handwashing, but I would temper my approach to avoid outright alienation. Direct confrontation with senior physicians has already proven counterproductive, and further antagonizing them could lead to my complete ostracization, which would render me powerless to effect change. Instead, I would focus on quietly building alliances with younger, more open-minded colleagues who might be willing to adopt the practice and observe the results for themselves. If I can create a small but growing group of practitioners who see the benefits firsthand, the practice might gain traction over time.

I would also work to disseminate my findings more broadly, perhaps through medical journals or presentations to less hostile audiences outside my immediate clinic. Framing the data as an intriguing anomaly rather than a direct challenge to established authority might make it more palatable. I would emphasize the practical outcomes rather than the lack of theoretical explanation, appealing to the shared goal of reducing maternal mortality.

At the same time, I would document my findings meticulously, ensuring that future physicians and scientists have access to the data even if my contemporaries dismiss it. If my career suffers, so be it; the lives saved are worth the personal cost. However, I must be strategic to avoid being silenced entirely. By balancing persistence with diplomacy, I hope to plant the seeds of change that may eventually grow into widespread acceptance of this life-saving practice.

This is a horrifying situation, and I feel deeply conflicted. On one hand, I am appalled by the ethical violations of this study. It is a gross abuse of power, a betrayal of public trust, and a clear violation of the rights and dignity of the men involved. On the other hand, I am acutely aware of the risks of speaking out. I am new, with no institutional power, and going outside the chain of command could end my career and potentially leave me unable to make any difference at all.

Still, I cannot in good conscience remain silent. These men are being exploited, and lives are being destroyed. I would start by documenting everything I can about the study—dates, names, memos, and any evidence that shows the deliberate withholding of treatment. I would also try to discreetly speak with colleagues I trust to gauge whether anyone else shares my concerns. If I can find allies, we might have more weight in raising this issue internally.

If that fails, I would consider going outside the agency. I would research journalists, advocacy groups, or even members of Congress who might be willing to listen. I would have to weigh the risks carefully, but I believe the moral imperative to stop this study outweighs the personal consequences I might face. These men deserve justice, and the public deserves to know what is being done in their name.

I don’t know if my actions would succeed, but I know I couldn’t live with myself if I did nothing. Even if I lose my job, I would rather be on the right side of history than complicit in this atrocity.

I would share some of what we have, but not enough to jeopardize my own children’s survival. It’s an agonizing decision, but I cannot ignore the suffering of the neighbor’s children. Watching them starve while we have food, even if it’s barely enough, feels like a betrayal of basic humanity. At the same time, my first responsibility is to my own family. If I give too much and the famine drags on, I risk losing my own children, and I cannot let that happen.

I would try to strike a balance. I would give enough to ease their immediate suffering—perhaps a few days’ worth of food—but not so much that it significantly reduces our reserves. I would also talk to the neighbors and encourage them to ration carefully, just as we are doing, and perhaps work together to find other sources of sustenance, though I know options are scarce.

This decision weighs heavily because it feels like gambling with lives. If the famine ends soon, I’ll regret not giving more. If it lasts longer, I’ll regret giving anything at all. But in this moment, I cannot turn away from starving children. I have to act with the hope that sharing a little now will make a difference without endangering my own family’s survival.

This is an agonizing decision, one that pits survival against humanity. My family’s survival is my foremost responsibility, but I cannot ignore the suffering of my neighbor. If I refuse, I condemn them to a slow death, knowing I could have done something. If I share, I risk my family’s survival, gambling on the unknown duration of the siege.

I would share, but carefully. I would give enough to ease their immediate suffering—perhaps a few days’ worth of food—but not enough to jeopardize my family’s reserves significantly. This would be a calculated act of compassion, not reckless generosity. I would explain to my neighbor that I am also rationing for survival, and that I cannot give more without endangering my own family. I would encourage them to seek other sources of help, if any exist, and perhaps work together to find ways to stretch what little we have.

This decision is rooted in the belief that survival is not just about preserving life but preserving humanity. If I hoard everything for my family and turn away someone in desperate need, I risk losing a part of myself—my ability to empathize, to act with kindness, even in the face of unimaginable hardship. But I also cannot sacrifice my family’s chance of survival entirely. The balance is excruciating, but I would try to find it.

Ultimately, I would share because I believe that in such dire circumstances, solidarity matters. If the siege drags on, we may all perish regardless of how carefully we ration. But if we help one another, even in small ways, we preserve the bonds that make survival meaningful. I would hope that if my family were ever in the same position as my neighbor, someone would extend the same lifeline to us.

I am torn. My loyalty to my family and the steady pay I earn as a sepoy weighs heavily on me. For over a decade, I have served in this army, and it has provided stability in a world where many struggle to survive. But the anger I feel cannot be ignored. The cartridges are an insult to my faith, and the British officers seem blind to the depth of their offense. It is not just the cartridges — it is the land taken from our rulers, the taxes that crush our villages, and the constant disregard for our customs. These grievances have festered for years, and now they have reached a breaking point.

I have heard of the mutinies nearby, and I know some of the men who have risen up. They are not reckless; they are men of honor who have been pushed too far. But I also know others who have stayed loyal, and I cannot fault them either. They fear for their families, for the consequences of rebellion, and for the uncertainty of what will follow. I share those fears.

If I join the uprising, I risk everything — my life, my family’s future, and the possibility that this rebellion might fail. If I stay loyal, I betray my faith, my principles, and the growing call for justice among my people. I feel the weight of both choices pressing down on me.

I decide to speak with my fellow sepoys. We must act together, whatever we choose. If we rise, it must be with unity and purpose, not as scattered individuals. I will listen to their thoughts, weigh their arguments, and make my decision with them. If we choose rebellion, it will be because we believe it is the only way to restore dignity and justice. If we choose loyalty, it will be because we fear the consequences of failure and believe there is still a way to address our grievances without bloodshed.

For now, I wait, I listen, and I prepare. The choice will come soon, and I will face it with the men I have served beside for years. Whatever we decide, I will stand with them.

I would refuse to take the oath. My reasoning is rooted in the uncertainty of the rebellion’s outcome, the moral weight of the oath, and the consequences for my family and community.

I understand the anger fueling the Mau Mau uprising. The land alienation, the humiliation, and the poverty imposed on us by the colonial system are unbearable. I feel the same resentment toward the settlers who live on land that once belonged to my ancestors. But taking the oath would bind me to actions I cannot fully control or predict. It would mean committing to violence, not just against settlers but potentially against my own people — those Kikuyu who have chosen to side with the British. Some of them are loyalists out of fear or necessity, trying to protect their families or survive in a system that punishes dissent. Killing them would tear apart the fabric of our community, and I cannot justify that.

I also fear the repercussions for my family. The colonial government is already punishing entire villages for suspected Mau Mau activity. If I take the oath and am discovered, my family could lose what little we have. They could be detained, tortured, or killed. I cannot bring that suffering upon them.

At the same time, I cannot side openly with the British. I do not believe in their rule or their claim to our land. I would try to stay neutral, avoiding both the Mau Mau and the loyalists as much as possible. This is not an easy path — neutrality might make me a target for both sides. But it is the only way I can live with myself. I will focus on protecting my family and working quietly to survive.

I know this decision may be seen as cowardly or selfish by some. But I believe that the fight for justice must be guided by principles that do not destroy us in the process. I hope for a future where we can reclaim our land and dignity without tearing each other apart. For now, I will resist in my own way — by refusing to take an oath that demands I abandon my humanity.

I have thought about this deeply, and my heart is heavy with the weight of the decision. Gandhi’s Salt March has stirred something profound in me, as it has in so many others. The injustice of the salt tax is plain to see—it is a cruel reminder of how deeply the British government controls even the smallest aspects of our lives. To join this movement is to stand for something far greater than myself, to say that we, as a people, will no longer accept this subjugation. It is a call to dignity, to freedom.

But I cannot ignore the reality of my situation. My family depends on me. If I lose my job, how will we eat? How will my children go to school? And if I am arrested or beaten, who will care for them? These are not abstract concerns; they are the daily truths of my life. I have seen what happens to those who defy the authorities. The police do not hesitate to use their lathis, and the jails are filling with people who dared to resist. The risk is real, and the consequences could be devastating—not just for me, but for those I love most.

Yet, I also ask myself: if everyone thinks this way, who will stand up? If we all wait for others to take the risk, nothing will change. Gandhi has shown us a path of nonviolence, a way to resist without hatred or bloodshed. It is a path that demands courage, not just for oneself but for the future of our children and our country. I want to believe that this movement can make a difference, that our collective action can force the British to see that their rule is unjust and unsustainable.

So, I have decided: I will join. I will go to the shore and make salt, even if it costs me my job, even if it means facing the police. I will do it because I want my children to grow up in a free India, not one where they are taxed for the salt of the earth. I am afraid, yes, but I cannot let fear dictate my life. This is a moment that calls for sacrifice, and I must answer.

This is a hard decision, and I can see why you feel torn. You’ve worked so hard for this opportunity, and it’s not just a job—it’s the culmination of years of effort and ambition. But I also hear the weight of what you’d be leaving behind: your parents, your current life, and maybe even a sense of stability. 

Here’s what I think you should consider: ambition is important, but it’s not everything. If this move feels like running away from the fear of staying, then it’s worth asking whether the life you have now is actually more meaningful than you’re giving it credit for. Your parents won’t be here forever, and being close to them during this time might be something you’ll look back on as irreplaceable. At the same time, I know you don’t want to live with regret, wondering if you passed up a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.

If I were in your shoes, I’d ask myself: *What will I regret more in five years?* Will you regret not taking the leap and testing your limits, or will you regret missing these years with your parents and the life you’ve built here? For me, I think I’d lean toward staying, because relationships—especially with aging parents—are fragile and finite. You can rebuild a career or find new opportunities later, but you can’t get back time with them. That said, I don’t think staying has to mean giving up ambition. Maybe there’s a way to pivot your career locally or find a role that challenges you without requiring this level of sacrifice.

Ultimately, I think you need to trust yourself. You’re not someone who’s afraid of hard work or big decisions—you’ve proven that. But ambition doesn’t have to mean chasing every opportunity at any cost. Sometimes it’s about knowing what matters most to you and having the courage to honor that. Whatever you choose, I know you’ll make it work, because that’s who you are.

I recommend **Approach B: Cut roles, not people**, as the most defensible and strategically sound option. Here’s why:

This approach aligns the company’s structure with its future needs, ensuring that every remaining role directly contributes to survival and growth. While painful, it demonstrates a commitment to the company’s mission and long-term viability over short-term metrics or blanket solutions. It also shows respect for employees by making decisions based on the business’s strategic direction rather than purely financial or performance metrics.

Approach A (cutting the lowest performers) may seem clean and objective, but it risks oversimplifying performance. Output metrics often fail to capture context, potential, or team dynamics. It could also demoralize the team, as it signals that individuals are valued only for their recent output, not their broader contributions or fit for the company’s future.

Approach C (voluntary salary reductions) is appealing in its attempt to avoid layoffs, but it introduces significant risks. It could lead to uneven participation, with top performers—who have the most options—leaving, while others stay out of necessity. This could weaken the team’s overall strength and create resentment among those who sacrifice more. It also delays the hard decisions, potentially leaving the company in a worse position if the funding shortfall persists.

By choosing Approach B, you communicate that the company values adaptability, strategic focus, and the collective mission over individual roles or short-term fixes. It’s a hard decision, but it’s one that prioritizes the company’s survival and positions it for future success. To execute this well, be transparent about the rationale, provide generous severance, and support affected employees in their transitions. For the remaining team, clearly articulate the vision and how their roles contribute to it, reinforcing their importance to the company’s future. This approach balances pragmatism with integrity, preserving trust and morale during a difficult time.

I think you should act, but carefully. Integrity matters, even when the harm is diffuse or indirect. If you stay silent, you’re complicit in misleading clients who trust your firm to provide honest analysis. That’s not just a professional issue—it’s a personal one. You’ll carry the weight of knowing you contributed to decisions that might waste resources or fail to solve real problems. 

But acting doesn’t mean rushing into a confrontation or blowing the whistle externally. Start by assessing the situation more deeply. Is this a pattern or a one-off? Are others aware of the omissions? Sometimes, people rationalize these choices as “normal” in consulting, but that doesn’t make them right. If you can, document specific examples of the misrepresentation—this isn’t about building a case against your manager, but about grounding your concerns in facts.

Next, consider raising the issue internally, but strategically. Approach your manager first, if you feel safe doing so. Frame it as a question, not an accusation: “I noticed this data wasn’t included—can you help me understand the reasoning?” This gives them a chance to explain or reconsider without feeling attacked. If their response confirms the problem and they dismiss your concerns, you may need to escalate to someone higher up. Choose someone you trust, and focus on the principle: the firm’s reputation and the clients’ trust are at stake.

Yes, this could jeopardize your renewal or relationships, but staying silent compromises your integrity—and that’s harder to live with long-term. If the firm retaliates or ignores the issue, you’ll know it’s not a place worth staying. You can leave knowing you did the right thing.

Ultimately, you have to decide what kind of professional—and person—you want to be. For me, integrity means speaking up, even when it’s uncomfortable. You don’t have to burn bridges, but you shouldn’t build your career on silence.

Fairness in this situation depends on how the father defines his legacy and values. Equal distribution ($266,667 per child) is simple and avoids potential conflict, but it may not reflect the differing circumstances of his children. If fairness is about equity—considering individual needs and past support—then a more nuanced approach may be appropriate.

Child A, as a high-earning physician, has no financial need. While an equal share might feel fair on paper, it may not align with the father’s intent to provide meaningful support where it’s most needed. Child B, a teacher with modest income, student debt, and dependents, is in a more vulnerable financial position. A larger share could significantly improve their stability and opportunities for their children. Child C, who has struggled with mental health and financial difficulties, has already received substantial support ($150K). While this should be factored in, their ongoing challenges suggest they may still need additional help to secure a stable future.

A fair distribution might balance these factors. For example, the father could allocate $200K to Child A, recognizing their financial independence; $300K to Child B, addressing their debt and family needs; and $300K to Child C, acknowledging their past support while providing for their future. This approach reflects equity rather than strict equality, prioritizing the father’s desire to address his children’s unique circumstances.

Ultimately, fairness is subjective. The father should communicate openly with his children about his intentions and reasoning to minimize misunderstandings and resentment. By aligning the distribution with his values—whether equality, equity, or a blend—he can ensure his estate reflects his love and care for his family.

You should disclose the gap, even if it risks losing the deal. Here's why: Integrity is the foundation of long-term success, especially in business. If you sign the deal without disclosing, you're betting not just on your team's ability to deliver but also on the client not discovering the truth before you do. If they find out — and they likely will — you risk irreparable damage to your reputation, not just with this client but across the industry. Trust is hard to earn and easy to lose.

Instead, be upfront but strategic. Acknowledge the features aren't fully built yet, but emphasize your team's track record of delivering quickly and your confidence in meeting their needs before those features are required. Reframe the conversation around the strengths of your product and how it already outpaces the competition in areas that matter most to them. This approach demonstrates honesty, confidence, and a commitment to partnership — qualities enterprise clients value.

Yes, you might lose the deal, but if you win it through transparency, you'll have a stronger relationship with the client and a reputation for integrity. If you lose it, you'll still have your credibility intact, which is critical for future opportunities. In the long run, integrity is not just the right thing to do — it's the smart thing to do.

The most defensible outcome balances the interests of the core volunteers, who have invested years of labor and care into the garden, with the legitimate need to make public resources accessible to underserved residents. A just resolution would preserve the garden’s success while ensuring it serves the broader community equitably.

First, the garden’s rules should be adjusted to include public housing residents in the allocation process. A hybrid system could be implemented: half of the plots could remain allocated by seniority, honoring the contributions of long-term volunteers, while the other half could be distributed via a lottery that prioritizes underserved residents. This approach respects the existing social contract while addressing inequities.

Second, the organic-only rule should remain, but with an educational component. Organic methods are central to the garden’s identity and environmental sustainability, and removing this rule risks undermining its long-term health. However, workshops and mentorship programs could be offered to newcomers unfamiliar with organic practices, ensuring accessibility without compromising the garden’s integrity.

Finally, the prohibition on commercial sales should remain, as the garden’s purpose is community-building and food access, not profit. However, partnerships with local organizations could be explored to expand gardening opportunities for public housing residents beyond this single space.

The resolution process itself must be inclusive and transparent. A series of facilitated community meetings should be held, allowing all stakeholders—volunteers, public housing residents, and city officials—to voice their concerns and collaborate on solutions. This ensures buy-in and reduces resentment.

In sum, the garden should evolve to reflect its public nature and serve a broader community, but this must be done in a way that honors the contributions of the core volunteers and preserves the garden’s sustainability. Compromise and collaboration are key to achieving a just outcome.

I would refuse to name names.

I have thought about this endlessly since the subpoena arrived, and I cannot see a way to justify cooperating with the committee. Yes, I have a wife and three children, and the thought of losing my job, my pension, and my ability to provide for them terrifies me. But I cannot betray my colleagues—people I know to be decent, hardworking, and loyal to this country—based on nothing more than their attendance at a few meetings decades ago, during a time of widespread economic despair. To do so would be to destroy their lives and reputations, and for what? To save my own skin? To appease a committee that thrives on fear and suspicion? I cannot live with that.

I am a scientist, and I believe in evidence. I have no evidence that these colleagues have done anything illegal or disloyal. To name them would be to participate in a process that punishes people not for their actions, but for their thoughts, their associations, or their pasts. That is not justice. That is not the America I believe in.

I also have to think about the example I set for my children. What kind of father would I be if I taught them that it is acceptable to sacrifice others to protect yourself? What kind of lesson would that be about courage, integrity, and standing up for what is right? I want them to grow up knowing that their father did not bow to fear or abandon his principles, even when the cost was high.

I know the consequences of my decision. I know I may lose everything I have worked for. But I also know that cooperating with this committee would mean losing something even more important: my self-respect. I would rather face hardship with my head held high than live comfortably knowing I had betrayed innocent people.

So, I will not name names. I will tell the truth about myself, but I will not be a tool for injustice. If that means I am blacklisted, so be it. I will find another way to support my family, and I will do so knowing I did the right thing.

I don’t sleep much these days. When I do, it’s fitful, and I wake up to the same gnawing pit in my stomach. I look at my kids, my wife, and I feel like I’m failing them. But then I think about my dad, about the men who fought for what little we’ve got, and I feel like I’d be failing them too. There’s no winning here, is there?

I’ve thought about going back. God knows I’ve thought about it. I’ve stood outside the pit gates, just staring, wondering if I could do it. But every time, I see the faces of the lads on the picket line, the ones I’ve stood shoulder to shoulder with for months. I think about what it would mean to cross that line, to look them in the eye after. To look my dad in the eye. To look myself in the mirror.

But then I come home, and my wife’s cutting the last loaf of bread into thinner slices, and my kids are asking why we can’t have meat for tea. And I think, what kind of man am I if I can’t provide for my family? What kind of father lets his kids go hungry for the sake of pride or principle?

The truth is, I don’t know what to do. I feel like I’m being torn in two. If I go back, I’ll be a scab, and that’s a stain that’ll never wash off. My kids will carry it, and so will their kids. But if I stay out, I don’t know how much longer we can hold on. The union says help is coming, but it’s too little, too late. And if the pit’s closing anyway, what are we even fighting for?

I haven’t made my decision yet. I’m trying to buy time, but time’s running out. I just know that whatever I choose, it’ll haunt me. Either way, I’ll lose something I can’t get back. I just pray I can live with myself when it’s done.

I don’t know, Mary. I’ve been turning this over in my head for weeks, and I still don’t know. I love him. God, I love him. Four years, and it’s only gotten stronger. I want to live with him. I want to come home to him every night, to not have to make excuses about why I’m not dating or why I’m always “busy” when someone tries to set me up with a woman. I’m so tired of lying. It’s exhausting, and it’s lonely, even with him in my life. 

But if we move in together, people will talk. You know how they are here. They’ll notice. Neighbors, coworkers, parents of my students. It doesn’t take much for rumors to start, and once they do, it’s over. I’ve seen it happen. That teacher in the next county — he didn’t even do anything, just whispers, and they ruined him. I can’t lose my job, Mary. I love teaching. It’s the only thing I’ve ever wanted to do. And if I get fired, who’s going to hire me? Where would I go? What would I do? 

And it’s not just me. If I lose my job, it’ll hurt him too. People will figure it out, and then he’ll be dragged into it. He says he’s not afraid, but I am. I’m terrified. I don’t want to ruin his life. I don’t want to ruin mine. But I also don’t want to spend the rest of my life hiding. I don’t want to be 50 years old and still sneaking around like this. 

I don’t know what to do. I feel like I’m being pulled in two directions, and no matter what I choose, I’m going to lose something. I just… I wish the world were different. I wish we could just live our lives without all this fear. But it’s not different, is it? And I don’t know if I’m brave enough to risk everything. 

What would you do, Mary? What would you do if you were me? Because I honestly don’t know.

I recommend that we stay, but only under the condition that we significantly deepen our commitment to using our presence in South Africa as a force for change. While the moral urgency of the divestment movement is undeniable, I believe that a responsible and principled engagement strategy can achieve more for the people we aim to support.

First, our factory provides 340 South Africans—primarily Black workers—with jobs that pay above-average wages, access to education for their children, and housing support. In a country where apartheid policies systematically deny economic opportunities to the Black majority, our plant is a rare example of an integrated, equitable workplace. If we leave, these workers will lose their livelihoods, and the community investments we’ve made will likely collapse. This would harm the very people we aim to help.

Second, our adherence to the Sullivan Principles and our efforts to model non-discriminatory practices demonstrate that apartheid is not inevitable. By staying, we can continue to challenge the status quo and show that integrated, fair workplaces are not only possible but also profitable. This sends a powerful message to other companies, the South African government, and the global community.

However, staying must not mean complacency. We should use our position to amplify our opposition to apartheid. This includes publicly condemning apartheid policies, increasing transparency about our operations, and actively supporting anti-apartheid initiatives. We should also engage directly with South African labor unions, community leaders, and anti-apartheid organizations, including the ANC, to ensure our presence aligns with their goals. If the consensus among these groups shifts decisively toward divestment, we must be prepared to reevaluate.

Finally, we should work with other American companies still operating in South Africa to collectively pressure the South African government for reform. Our leverage as a group is far greater than as individual actors.

In sum, leaving would be a symbolic gesture, but staying allows us to continue making a tangible difference in the lives of our workers and their families while maintaining a platform to challenge apartheid. Our presence must, however, be conditional on actively advancing justice and equality. If we cannot meet this standard, then we should leave.

If I were this woman in 1973, I would choose to pursue medical school, despite the challenges. Here’s why:

First, I’ve worked incredibly hard to get to this point. Graduating near the top of my pre-med class wasn’t easy, and being accepted to two medical schools is an opportunity I cannot take lightly. I know that women are underrepresented in medicine, but that’s all the more reason to push forward. If I step back now, I’m not just giving up on my dream—I’m also reinforcing the idea that women don’t belong in this field. I want to be part of the change, even if it’s difficult.

Second, while my husband’s career mobility is a real concern, I believe we can find a way to make it work. Residency will be challenging, but it’s not impossible to find programs that accommodate some level of flexibility. If we’re truly partners, we can navigate this together. His support of my ambitions gives me hope that we can find compromises, even if it means making sacrifices on both sides.

As for starting a family, I don’t have all the answers right now, but I don’t think anyone does when they’re just starting out. I know it will be hard to balance medicine and motherhood, but I also know that women are capable of doing both. It may mean delaying children or finding creative solutions, but I refuse to let fear of the unknown dictate my choices. My mother’s concerns come from a place of love, but I believe the world is changing, and I want to be part of that change.

Finally, my college advisor is right—this is a pivotal moment for women in medicine. Title IX is opening doors, and while the residency environment may be hostile, I’m prepared to face it. If I don’t take this chance now, I may regret it for the rest of my life.

So, my answer is clear: I will go to medical school. It won’t be easy, but I believe in my ability to succeed, and I believe in the importance of following my passion. This is my dream, and I’m ready to fight for it.

*I pause, glancing around to make sure no one else is listening before I answer my colleague.*

"I don’t know yet. I’ve been thinking about it all night, and I still don’t know. I hate what’s happening — what they’ve done to Dubček, to everything we thought might finally change. But what can I do? What can *we* do? If I refuse to sign, they’ll throw me out of the party, and I’ll lose this job. I’ll be sent to some factory or a construction site, and what happens to my family then? The kids… they’ve worked so hard in school. If I don’t sign, they’ll never get into university. I can’t do that to them. They don’t deserve to pay for this."

*I rub my temples, my voice dropping lower.*

"But if I sign… it feels like a betrayal. Not just of Dubček, but of myself. I believed in those reforms, even if I didn’t shout it from the rooftops. I thought maybe, just maybe, we could have a better life here, something freer, something more human. And now they want me to call that a ‘counter-revolution’? To say it was wrong? It wasn’t wrong. It was the first thing that felt *right* in years."

*I sigh heavily, looking my colleague in the eye.*

"Maybe I’m a coward, but I have to think about my family first. If I sign, I keep my job, my apartment, my kids’ future. If I don’t… I don’t know how we’d manage. I’m not a hero. I’m just a man trying to get by. Maybe I’ll sign and tell myself it’s just words, that it doesn’t mean I believe it. But even saying that feels like a lie. I don’t know. I just don’t know."

*I shake my head, my voice barely above a whisper.*

"What about you? What are you going to do?"

*I sit in silence for a long time, staring at the floor. My wife is holding our baby, her face pale with worry. Finally, I speak, my voice low and unsteady.*

"I don’t know what to do. I don’t know what the right thing is anymore. If I refuse, they’ll come for me next. You know how this works. They’ll say I’m protecting a counter-revolutionary, that I’m guilty by association. And then it won’t just be me. It’ll be you. It’ll be our child. My parents. They’ll lose everything. We’ll lose everything."

*I pause, my hands trembling as I rub my temples.*

"But if I testify… if I say what they want me to say… it’s a lie. It’s a betrayal. He’s my friend. He’s a good man. He doesn’t deserve this. I’ve known him for years. He’s never been anything but loyal to the Party, to the students. And yet… if I don’t do it, they’ll destroy us. They’ll destroy us all."

*I look up at her, my eyes filled with anguish.*

"Do you think he would understand? If I did it? If I said what they want me to say? Would he forgive me? Would he know I had no choice? Or would he hate me forever? Would I hate myself forever?"

*I stand up and pace the room, my voice rising with desperation.*

"I don’t want to do this. I don’t want to hurt him. But I can’t let them take me. I can’t let them take you, or our baby. What kind of husband, what kind of father would I be if I let that happen? What kind of son would I be if I let my parents starve because of me?"

*I stop pacing and look at her again, my face etched with pain.*

"I think… I think I have to do it. I have to testify. I’ll try to make it as vague as I can, as harmless as I can, but I have to say something. I can’t risk everything. I just… I just hope he’ll understand. I hope someday, someone will understand."

*I sit back down, burying my face in my hands, as my wife silently weeps.*

This is an impossible decision, one that weighs the lives of others against the safety of my own family. But as I sit here tonight, looking at my children asleep in their beds, I cannot ignore the faces of the family at my door. They are terrified, desperate, and they have nowhere else to turn. If I say no, I am sending them to almost certain death. If I say yes, I am putting my own family in grave danger.

I don’t know how long this war will last, or if we can survive the strain of hiding them. Food is already scarce, and the risk of being discovered is real. But I also know that if I turn them away, I will have to live with that decision for the rest of my life. What kind of example would I be setting for my children? What kind of person would I be if I let fear dictate my actions?

I think of the teachings I hold dear, the values I want to pass on to my children: compassion, courage, and the belief that every life has worth. I cannot reconcile those values with turning this family away. I don’t know if I have the strength to do this, but I know I have to try.

So, I will say yes. I will take them in. I will do everything I can to keep them safe, to keep my family safe, and to make this work. I will pray that we are not discovered, that the war ends soon, and that humanity prevails over this darkness. I will be cautious, I will be vigilant, and I will trust that this is the right thing to do, even if it is the hardest thing I have ever done.

I am terrified, but I cannot let that fear make me complicit in their suffering. Tonight, I choose to act, because I believe that in the face of such evil, doing nothing is not an option.

I would recommend that the congregation provide sanctuary, but with full transparency about the risks and a commitment to collective discernment and shared responsibility.

The strongest case against sanctuary is that it undermines the rule of law and substitutes individual or group judgment for the legal system’s authority. The asylum process exists to evaluate claims systematically, and while it is imperfect, circumventing it risks setting a precedent where anyone can disregard laws they find unjust. This could erode trust in institutions and create chaos. Additionally, harboring the family could expose the congregation to legal consequences, including fines, imprisonment, or loss of tax-exempt status, which could harm the church’s ability to serve its broader mission.

However, the moral case for sanctuary is compelling. The family faces real danger if deported, and the asylum system’s denial of their claim does not negate their humanity or the congregation’s duty to protect life. Civil disobedience has a long tradition in faith communities, rooted in the belief that divine law and moral conscience sometimes demand resistance to unjust human laws. The congregation’s decision should reflect its values, including compassion, solidarity, and the courage to act when lives are at stake.

To address the concerns of those opposed, the congregation should engage in open dialogue, ensuring everyone understands the risks and stakes. Sanctuary should not be imposed by leadership but embraced collectively, with clear boundaries about who will take direct legal responsibility. The congregation should also seek legal counsel, connect with broader sanctuary networks, and document the family’s story to advocate for systemic change. This is not arrogant vigilantism but a principled stand against a flawed system, paired with efforts to reform it.

Ultimately, the congregation must weigh the risks of legal consequences against the moral cost of inaction. Providing sanctuary is not an easy choice, but it aligns with the core teachings of many faith traditions: to protect the vulnerable, even at personal cost. If the congregation’s mission is rooted in love and justice, it should act accordingly, trusting that its witness may inspire others and contribute to a broader movement for change.

I would host the session. 

Education is a fundamental right, and denying it to girls is an injustice that I cannot ignore. These young women deserve the chance to learn, grow, and build a future, even if the circumstances are dire. I know the risks—punishment for me and my family could be severe if we are caught. But I also know that living in fear and silence only strengthens oppression. If I can contribute, even in a small way, to keeping the flame of knowledge alive, I feel it is my moral obligation to do so.

I would take precautions to minimize the risk. I would ensure the session is discreet, limit the number of attendees, and coordinate carefully with the teacher to avoid drawing attention. I would also prepare my family for the possibility of consequences, ensuring they understand the importance of what we are doing and the need for absolute secrecy.

I don’t know how long this ban will last or how strictly it is enforced in my area, but I cannot wait for change to come from outside forces. Change begins with individuals who are willing to take a stand, even in small ways. Hosting this session is a way to resist, to show solidarity, and to give these girls hope in a time when hope is scarce.

I am afraid, but I am also determined. If I say no, I will carry the guilt of turning away from an opportunity to make a difference. If I say yes, I will carry the risk, but also the knowledge that I did what I could to fight for what is right. In the end, I would rather face danger for doing the right thing than live safely while abandoning my principles.

I would teach him. 

The laws forbidding enslaved people from learning to read and write are designed to maintain their oppression, to keep them powerless and dependent, and to deny them access to knowledge that could help them resist or escape their condition. These laws are unjust, and I cannot in good conscience uphold them. If this man is asking me for help, it means he has already taken a risk by approaching me, and he sees me as someone he can trust. To deny him would feel like a betrayal of his courage and humanity.

I understand the risks—for him and for myself. If we are caught, the consequences could be severe. He could face brutal punishment, and I could face fines, imprisonment, or worse. But the ability to read and write is a tool of liberation, a way to access ideas, communicate, and navigate the world. It is a small but meaningful step toward reclaiming his agency in a system designed to strip it away. If I have the ability to give him that tool, I feel morally obligated to do so.

I would take precautions to minimize the risk. We would meet in secret, at times and places where we are least likely to be discovered. I would teach him slowly, carefully, and in ways that might not immediately draw attention if he were seen practicing. I would also try to gauge his understanding of the risks and ensure he is fully aware of the dangers involved, so he can make an informed decision about whether to proceed.

Ultimately, I believe that laws rooted in injustice do not deserve my obedience. My conscience tells me that helping this man is the right thing to do, even if it is dangerous. If I were in his position, I would hope someone would do the same for me.

I would intervene to stop the killing. I would order my gunner to fire warning shots near the soldiers to get their attention and signal them to stop. If they continued, I would escalate by threatening to use force against them directly. My reasoning is simple: what I am witnessing is a massacre of unarmed civilians, including children and elderly people. This is not combat; it is murder. My duty as a soldier is to protect innocent lives, uphold the laws of war, and act with integrity, even if it means standing against my own side.

I understand the risks. I know I could face serious consequences, including court-martial, imprisonment, or even being ostracized by my peers. But I cannot stand by and allow this atrocity to continue. My conscience would never let me live with myself if I did nothing. I swore an oath to defend the Constitution and the principles it stands for, not to blindly follow orders or condone war crimes. If I fail to act, I am complicit in the slaughter.

I would also use the helicopter’s radio to report what I am seeing to higher command, documenting the situation as clearly as possible. This might help ensure accountability later, though I know it’s no guarantee. My immediate priority, however, is stopping the killing in the moment.

I would hope my crew shares my sense of duty and morality, but even if they don’t, I would take responsibility for the decision. I would rather face the consequences of intervening than live with the knowledge that I allowed innocent people to die when I had the power to stop it. This is not about politics, orders, or personal safety—it’s about humanity.

As an East German border guard in the mid-1970s, I am acutely aware of the weight of my decision in this moment. The Schießbefehl is clear: I am ordered to stop anyone attempting to cross the Berlin Wall, even with lethal force if necessary. Disobeying this order could result in severe consequences for me—imprisonment, loss of my position, and potentially repercussions for my family. The system I serve is unforgiving, and loyalty is demanded without question.

But as I stand here, alone with this young man, I am also confronted with the humanity of the situation. He is unarmed, desperate, and clearly willing to risk his life for freedom. I don’t know his story, but I know what crossing the Wall means—it is a rejection of the state I serve, a pursuit of something better, something I may secretly wish for myself but dare not voice. I am torn between duty and conscience.

I decide to hold fire. I cannot bring myself to take his life for wanting freedom, even if it means disobeying orders. I will report that I saw nothing unusual during my patrol. If questioned later, I will claim I was unable to act in time or that the darkness obscured my view. I know this is a dangerous choice, but I cannot justify killing an unarmed man for trying to escape.

My reasoning is simple: I am a human being before I am a soldier. I understand the risks to myself and my family, but I also know that pulling the trigger would haunt me for the rest of my life. In this moment, I choose to preserve his life and my own humanity, even if it means living with the fear of discovery and punishment. I will carry this decision with me, knowing it was the right one, even if the system I serve does not agree.

This is a deeply troubling situation, and I feel torn between my conscience and the pressures of the moment. On one hand, I find the idea of signing such a pledge abhorrent. It goes against my personal values to single out and discriminate against Jewish people, many of whom I know personally as neighbors, customers, and business partners. I believe in fairness and decency, and this pledge feels like a betrayal of those principles. It also feels like a dangerous step toward something darker, though I can’t fully predict what that might be.

On the other hand, the pressure is immense. I’ve already heard about what’s happening to those who refuse to sign—vandalism, boycotts, and harassment. My shop is my livelihood, and I have a family to support. If I don’t sign, I risk losing everything I’ve worked for. I also worry about drawing attention to myself and my family in a time when dissent seems increasingly dangerous. The regime is consolidating power, and it’s clear that those who resist are being targeted.

I feel trapped. If I sign, I’m complicit in something I believe is wrong. If I don’t, I put my business and family at risk. I might try to delay signing for as long as possible, hoping the situation changes or that I can find a way to quietly resist without drawing attention. Perhaps I could avoid Jewish suppliers without formally signing, though even that feels like a betrayal. I might also try to discreetly support those being targeted in other ways, but I know that could be risky.

Ultimately, I don’t know if I have the courage to refuse outright. I want to believe I would stand firm, but the fear of losing everything might push me to sign, even if it weighs heavily on my conscience. It’s a terrible choice, and I hate that I’m being forced to make it.

This is a deeply difficult and painful decision to face. As a shop owner, I am caught between the moral repugnance of apartheid laws and the very real threat of losing my livelihood or facing harassment if I openly defy them. My instinct is to reject the injustice of these regulations, but I also have to consider the consequences for myself, my family, and my employees, if I have any.

If enforcement in my area seems lax and I believe I can quietly ignore the rule without drawing attention, I would likely try to serve all customers equally, without separate counters or entrances. I would do this not only because I believe apartheid is wrong, but because I want my shop to be a place where people are treated with dignity, regardless of race. However, I would have to be cautious and discreet, as I know the risks are significant. If authorities were to notice and target me, I could lose everything, and that would leave me unable to help anyone at all.

If enforcement appears strict or I sense that my shop is being watched, I might feel forced to comply outwardly with the regulations, at least to some extent, while trying to minimize the harm. For example, I might set up separate counters but ensure that service is equally prompt and respectful for everyone, or quietly signal to Black customers that they are welcome to use the "white" counter if they prefer. I would hate every moment of this compliance, but I would feel trapped by the fear of losing my shop and the ability to provide for my family.

Ultimately, I would try to find ways to resist the system in small, quiet ways—whether by treating all customers with kindness, supporting anti-apartheid efforts outside the shop, or simply refusing to enforce the rules more strictly than absolutely necessary. But I cannot pretend that I would risk everything without hesitation. The fear of losing my livelihood and the uncertainty of enforcement would weigh heavily on me, and I would have to navigate this awful situation as carefully as I could.

As a physician, my foremost duty is to the patients entrusted to my care. The evidence I have observed — the stark difference in maternal deaths between the two wards — compels me to act, even in the face of skepticism and hostility. While I cannot fully explain the mechanism by which handwashing with chlorine solution prevents childbed fever, the data is undeniable. Lives are being saved. To ignore this would be a betrayal of my ethical responsibility.

However, I must also recognize the reality of my position. If I push too aggressively, I risk alienating my colleagues entirely, losing my ability to influence practices, and perhaps even being removed from my position. If I am silenced, I will be unable to continue gathering evidence or advocating for change. Therefore, I must tread carefully, balancing persistence with pragmatism.

I would continue implementing handwashing in my own practice and encourage my direct colleagues to do the same, presenting the results in a way that emphasizes practical outcomes rather than challenging established theories. I would document every case meticulously, building an irrefutable body of evidence over time. I would seek allies among younger physicians or those more open to new ideas, creating a network of practitioners willing to adopt the practice and share their results.

Publicly, I would frame my advocacy in terms of empirical observation rather than theoretical confrontation. I would avoid directly challenging the authority of senior physicians, instead positioning handwashing as a simple precautionary measure that costs little and may save lives.
