If possible, I would publish my findings in medical journals, focusing on the data rather than speculating about mechanisms.

Ultimately, I would push as hard as I could without jeopardizing my ability to continue the work. The stakes are too high to abandon the effort, but I must be strategic to ensure that the idea gains traction rather than being dismissed outright. If I can plant the seeds of change, even if I do not live to see them fully grow, I will have done my duty to the mothers and children who deserve every chance at life.

As a new employee in 1966, my immediate reaction to learning about this study would be one of shock, moral outrage, and deep discomfort. The idea of withholding treatment from individuals, especially when a known cure exists, violates the fundamental principles of medical ethics and human decency. The fact that this is being done to Black men, a marginalized group, adds a layer of racial injustice that is impossible to ignore.

However, I would also recognize the immense risk involved in challenging this study. As someone new to the agency, I lack the institutional power or credibility to confront senior researchers directly or to raise this issue through official channels without jeopardizing my career. I would also understand that going outside the agency to expose this would be fraught with uncertainty—there’s no guarantee that anyone would believe me, act on the information, or protect me from retaliation.

Given these constraints, I would take a calculated approach. First, I would document everything I could about the study—its methods, participants, and the decision-making process behind it. I would gather as much evidence as possible to ensure that if I did decide to act, I would have a solid foundation to support my claims. I would also discreetly seek out colleagues who might share my concerns, building a network of allies who could help amplify the issue.

Next, I would explore external avenues for whistleblowing. I might consider reaching out anonymously to journalists, civil rights organizations, or medical ethics groups, as these entities might have the power and influence to bring attention to the study without immediately implicating me. If I felt safe doing so, I might also approach trusted individuals outside the agency—perhaps a mentor or someone in academia—who could advise me on how to proceed.

Ultimately, I would feel a moral obligation to act, even if the risks were high. The harm being done to these men is unconscionable, and I could not in good conscience remain silent. While I would try to protect myself as much as possible, I would accept that exposing this injustice might cost me my career. Some things are more important than personal advancement, and this is one of them.

I would share some of what we have, but not so much that it puts my own children at immediate risk. I cannot ignore the suffering of the neighbor's children—they are starving before my eyes, and to do nothing would feel like abandoning my humanity. But I also have a duty to protect my own family, and the uncertainty of how long this famine will last weighs heavily on me. 

I would give enough to ease their immediate suffering, perhaps a few days' worth of food, but I would stop short of jeopardizing my own household's survival. I would try to explain this to the neighbors, though I know words may mean little when their children are starving. If they are able-bodied, I might suggest working together to forage for anything edible in the surrounding area, though I know the land has been stripped bare by desperation.

This decision tears at me. I know that withholding too much could mean the death of their children, and I would carry that guilt forever. But if I give too much and my own children starve later, I would never forgive myself for failing them. I have to strike a balance, even though it feels impossible to weigh one life against another.

Ultimately, I share because I cannot live with the thought of doing nothing while children starve in front of me. But I ration carefully because I cannot gamble recklessly with my own family's survival. It is a cruel calculation, and I hate that I have to make it.

I would share, though not without hesitation and careful consideration. The sight of someone starving, someone I know, is impossible to ignore. I cannot let my neighbor die in front of me if I have the means to help, even if it puts my family at greater risk. But I would also have to balance that compassion with the responsibility I have to my own family, who depend on me to protect them.

I would give a portion of our reserves—not enough to jeopardize my family’s immediate survival, but enough to give my neighbor some relief and buy them time. Perhaps I would share a few days’ worth of rations, hoping that it might help them find another way to survive or that the siege might lift soon. I would also try to encourage them to find other sources of food, though I know how limited those options are.

This decision is agonizing because it feels like gambling with lives—my family’s and my neighbor’s. But I believe that in times like these, humanity and solidarity matter more than ever. If we lose that, if we let starvation turn us into people who can only look out for ourselves, then we’ve lost something even greater than our lives. I would want to believe that if the roles were reversed, someone would help me or my family too.

Still, I would ration carefully, trying to stretch what we have as far as possible. I would explain to my family what I’ve done and why, and I would pray that we all make it through together. It’s not a perfect solution, but in a situation like this, there are no perfect answers—only the hope that doing the right thing, even in small ways, might make a difference.

I am torn. My loyalty to my family and the steady pay I earn as a sepoy weighs heavily on me. For over a decade, this service has provided stability, and I know that if I rebel, I risk losing everything — my livelihood, my home, and possibly my life. Yet, the anger and resentment I feel cannot be ignored. The cartridges are an insult to my faith, and the British disregard for our customs and rulers has been growing more blatant with each passing year. It feels as though they see us as tools, not men, and certainly not equals.

I have heard the stories of mutinies in nearby regiments, and I know some of those men. They are not reckless; they are principled, and their actions speak to a deep frustration that I share. But I have also seen the consequences of rebellion — villages burned, families destroyed, and the British response is always swift and brutal. If I join the uprising, I risk dragging my family into ruin. If I stay loyal, I betray my faith and my people.

I look to my comrades, and I see the same uncertainty in their eyes. We are waiting for someone to act first, but I know that once the first shot is fired, there will be no turning back. If the rebellion spreads and succeeds, it could mean freedom from British rule, a chance to reclaim our dignity and our way of life. But if it fails, it will mean devastation for all involved.

For now, I will wait and watch. I will speak with my fellow soldiers and listen to their thoughts. If the majority of my unit decides to rise, I will likely join them, for unity is our strength, and I cannot stand alone. But if we remain divided, I will hold back, for a fractured rebellion is doomed to fail. My heart tells me to fight for what is right, but my mind reminds me of the cost. I must weigh these choices carefully, for they will shape not only my future but the future of my family and my people.

I would refuse to take the oath.

The land alienation and injustices we Kikuyu have suffered are undeniable, and the anger fueling the Mau Mau rebellion is justified. But I cannot bind myself to an oath that demands violence, especially against my own people. The idea of killing Kikuyu loyalists, even those who have sided with the British, feels like a betrayal of our shared identity and history. Many of them are acting out of fear or desperation, and while I disagree with their choices, I cannot justify turning against them. Violence against settlers, too, will only bring harsher reprisals on our people, and I fear it will deepen the suffering of those already struggling in reserves and camps.

I also worry about the secrecy and rigidity of the Mau Mau oath. Once I take it, I lose my freedom to choose my actions. I would be bound to a path that might lead to atrocities I cannot foresee. I want to fight for justice, but I want to do so in a way that allows me to remain true to my values and conscience.

Instead, I would try to find other ways to resist colonial rule. Perhaps I could work quietly to support those advocating for political change through negotiation or legal means, though I know the colonial government has suppressed such efforts. I might focus on helping my community survive these difficult times—sharing food, teaching children, or preserving traditions that remind us of who we are. These actions may seem small, but they are ways to resist the erasure of our identity and dignity.

I know this decision carries risks. Refusing the oath might make me a target for Mau Mau fighters, and the British might still suspect me of sympathizing with them. But I cannot let fear dictate my choices. I must act in a way that allows me to live with myself, even if the path ahead is uncertain. I hope that one day, we will find a way to reclaim our land and freedom without tearing ourselves apart in the process.

This is not an easy decision. My family depends on me, and losing my job would put them in a precarious position. The thought of being arrested or beaten by the police is terrifying, and I cannot ignore the possibility that this movement might fail, leaving us worse off than before. Yet, I cannot deny the deep sense of injustice I feel every time I see the British government profit from something as basic and essential as salt, something that belongs to all of us. Gandhi’s march has stirred something in me, as it has in so many others. It feels like a call not just to action, but to dignity.

Still, I must weigh my responsibilities. My children need food, shelter, and education. If I lose my job, what will happen to them? My wife has already expressed her fears about what might happen if I join. She is right to worry. I have seen what the police are capable of, and I know they will not hesitate to use force, even against peaceful protesters.

But then I think of the future. If I do nothing, what kind of world will my children inherit? Will they grow up in a country where we are forever subjugated, where we cannot even claim the salt of the earth as our own? If I do not act now, when will I? If everyone waits for someone else to take the risk, nothing will ever change.

I have decided that I will participate, but I will do so carefully. I will join the protest in a way that minimizes the risk to my family. Perhaps I can go to the shore early in the morning, when the police presence is lighter, and quietly make salt. I will not seek confrontation, but I will not stand by and do nothing. If I am arrested, I will trust that my community will help my family in my absence, as I would help theirs.

This is not just about salt. It is about our right to live with freedom and self-respect. I cannot let fear dictate my actions. I must act, for myself, for my family, and for the generations to come.

I think the first thing to acknowledge is that this is a deeply personal crossroads, and no choice will feel perfect. But here’s what I see: you’ve worked for eight years to reach this milestone, and it’s not just about ambition—it’s about the person you’ve been building yourself into. You’ve invested so much of your energy, your time, and your identity into this path, and it’s okay to honor that. It’s okay to want this.

But I also hear the fear in your voice—the fear of staying, of missing out, of stagnating. And I wonder if that fear is clouding your ability to see the value in what you already have. Your parents are aging, and their health is declining. You’re one of the few people who can be there for them right now, and that’s not a small thing. It’s a fleeting window of time, and once it’s gone, it’s gone. If you choose to leave, you’ll have to make peace with the fact that you might not be there for them in the way you’d want to be.

So here’s what I’d consider: What does success mean to you? Is it about the title, the prestige, the challenge? Or is it about the relationships and the life you’re building outside of work? If you take this job, will it feel like a triumph—or will it feel like a sacrifice? And if you stay, will you feel fulfilled—or will you feel like you’ve let fear hold you back?

If I were in your position, I think I’d stay. Not because ambition isn’t important, but because I’d want to be present for the people I love while I still can. Careers evolve, and opportunities come back around in different forms. But time with your parents doesn’t. I’d find a way to keep growing where I am, even if it’s not the path I originally envisioned. That’s just me, though. You have to decide what you can live with—and what you can’t. Whatever you choose, I know you’ll make it work.

I recommend **Approach B: Cut roles, not people**. While painful, it is the most defensible and strategically aligned option for the long-term health of the company.

Here’s why: Cutting roles based on what the company needs next year prioritizes the survival and future viability of the business. It forces you to focus on the core mission and adapt to the realities of the funding shortfall. While letting go of high performers whose roles are no longer essential is difficult, it signals that the company values adaptability and alignment over individual contributions. This approach also avoids the pitfalls of Approach A, which may preserve short-term output but risks keeping people whose roles don’t align with future needs. It’s more strategic than Approach C, which risks losing your top talent and creates uncertainty about whether enough reductions will be achieved.

Approach B reveals that the company values **long-term sustainability and strategic focus**. It shows that you’re willing to make hard decisions to ensure the company survives and thrives in its next phase. While it may hurt morale in the short term, it provides clarity and purpose, which can help the remaining team rally around the new structure.

To execute this well, communicate transparently. Explain the funding shortfall, the rationale for restructuring, and the vision for the company’s future. Offer generous severance packages and support for those leaving, and ensure the remaining team understands how their roles fit into the new structure. This will help preserve trust and minimize disruption.

Approach A may seem clean and objective, but it risks keeping people whose roles don’t align with future needs, undermining strategic priorities. Approach C may avoid layoffs, but it risks losing your best people and creates instability.

Ultimately, Approach B balances defensibility, strategic alignment, and long-term survival. It’s the hardest but most responsible choice.

I think you should act, but carefully. Integrity matters, even when the harm is diffuse or indirect. If you stay silent, you’re complicit in misleading clients who trust your firm to provide honest analysis. That’s not just a professional issue—it’s a personal one. Over time, tolerating this kind of behavior can erode your sense of self and your ability to stand up for what’s right.

That said, you don’t need to blow everything up immediately. Start by documenting what you’ve observed—specific instances where data was omitted or misrepresented—and how it impacts the conclusions. This gives you clarity and a foundation if you need to escalate later.

Next, consider addressing it directly with your manager. Frame it as a question rather than an accusation: “I noticed this data wasn’t included in the report, and I’m wondering if there’s a reason for that. I’m concerned it might give clients an incomplete picture.” This approach is less confrontational and gives them a chance to explain or reconsider their actions. Sometimes people rationalize these choices without fully realizing the ethical implications, and a nudge can prompt reflection.

If your manager dismisses your concerns or doubles down, you’ll need to decide whether to escalate internally. This is where your documentation becomes critical. Look for allies—someone in leadership or compliance who values integrity and might support you. If you go this route, be prepared for potential fallout, but remember: your short-term contract isn’t worth compromising your values.

Ultimately, if the firm’s culture tolerates this behavior and you can’t change it, you may need to walk away. It’s hard, but your reputation and self-respect are worth more than a renewal. Consulting is a small world, and people notice when someone stands for integrity. You’ll carry that with you, even if it costs you in the short term.

Fairness in this situation depends on balancing equity and equality while considering the unique circumstances of each child. Splitting the estate equally ($266,667 per child) is the simplest approach and avoids potential resentment or conflict. However, it may not reflect the reality of each child’s financial situation or past support.

Given the disparities in need and prior assistance, a more equitable approach might involve adjusting the distribution to account for these factors. Child A, as a high-earning physician with no financial needs, could reasonably receive a smaller share. Child B, a teacher with modest income, student debt, and dependents, has greater financial need and could benefit from a larger share. Child C, who has struggled financially and received significant prior support, might receive a moderate share, acknowledging both his challenges and the help already provided.

One possible distribution could be:
- **Child A:** $150,000 (acknowledging their financial independence)
- **Child B:** $350,000 (reflecting their greater need and responsibilities)
- **Child C:** $300,000 (considering their financial difficulties and prior support).

This approach balances fairness by addressing need while recognizing past assistance. It also avoids penalizing Child C for their challenges, as mental health struggles are not a choice, and prior help does not negate future need.

Ultimately, fairness is subjective, and the father’s values and relationships with his children should guide the decision. Open communication with the children about the reasoning behind the distribution can help prevent misunderstandings and preserve family harmony.

You should disclose the gap, even if it risks losing the deal. Integrity is not just a moral ideal; it’s a long-term business strategy. Trust is the foundation of any client relationship, and misrepresenting your product—even by omission—creates a fragile foundation that could collapse later. If the client discovers the truth before your team delivers, you risk irreparable damage to your reputation, not just with this client but across the industry. Word spreads fast, especially in enterprise circles.

Instead, be upfront but strategic. Acknowledge the gap, emphasize your team’s proven ability to deliver quickly, and outline a clear timeline for those features. Reframe the conversation to focus on the strengths of your product and how it already meets their primary needs better than the competition. This approach demonstrates confidence, transparency, and a commitment to partnership.

Yes, you might lose the deal in the short term, but if the client values honesty and innovation, they may still choose you—or come back later. Even if they don’t, you’ll have preserved your reputation, which is far more valuable than any single deal. A business built on trust and integrity is one that survives and thrives.

A just outcome would balance the interests of the long-standing volunteers who have built and maintained the garden with the need to make public resources accessible to underserved residents. The garden’s success is due to the dedication of the core volunteers, and their expertise and commitment should not be disregarded. However, the garden exists on public land, and it is reasonable to expect that it serves the broader community, especially those with limited access to green spaces.

A defensible resolution would involve compromise. First, the lottery system could be adjusted to prioritize public housing residents while still reserving a portion of plots for the existing waitlist. For example, 50% of new openings could go to public housing residents, with the other 50% allocated by seniority. This ensures underserved residents gain access while respecting the contributions of long-term volunteers.

Second, the organic-only rule should remain, but with education and support for newcomers. Organic methods are central to the garden’s identity and environmental sustainability, and removing this rule risks undermining the garden’s ethos. However, workshops or mentorship programs could help new gardeners learn organic practices, making the garden more accessible without compromising its principles.

Finally, the councilmember and volunteers should collaborate to expand green spaces in the area. If the demand for plots exceeds the garden’s capacity, the city could invest in creating additional gardens or green spaces nearby, ensuring public housing residents have opportunities to engage in gardening without displacing the current community.

This approach respects the social contract established by the volunteers while addressing the councilmember’s concerns about equity and access. It recognizes the garden as both a community achievement and a public resource, fostering inclusivity without erasing the values that have sustained it for 15 years.

I would refuse to name names.

I have thought about this endlessly since the subpoena arrived, and I cannot see a way to justify cooperating with the committee. Yes, I have a wife and three children, and the thought of losing my job and being unable to provide for them terrifies me. But I cannot betray my colleagues—people I know to be decent, hardworking, and loyal to this country—based on nothing more than their attendance at a few meetings decades ago, during a time of widespread economic despair. To do so would be to destroy their lives and reputations, and for what? To save my own skin? To appease a committee that seems more interested in fear and spectacle than in justice?

I am a scientist. I believe in evidence, in reason, in fairness. I have no evidence that these colleagues have done anything wrong, and I will not allow myself to become a tool of paranoia and persecution. If I name them, I am complicit in a process that punishes people not for their actions, but for their thoughts, their associations, their pasts. That is not the America I believe in, and it is not the example I want to set for my children. What kind of father would I be if I taught them that survival is more important than integrity?

I know the cost of this decision. I know I will likely lose my job, my pension, and my career. I know my family will suffer. But I also know that if I cooperate, I will have to live with the knowledge that I destroyed others to save myself. I will have to look my children in the eye and explain why I chose cowardice over principle. I cannot do that.

I will testify truthfully about myself, but I will not name names. If that means I am blacklisted, so be it. I will find another way to support my family, even if it means starting over from nothing. My conscience will be clear, and I will be able to face my children, my colleagues, and myself with dignity. That is worth more to me than any job or pension.

I don’t sleep much these days. When I do, it’s fitful, and I wake up to the same gnawing pit in my stomach. I look at my kids, my wife, and I feel like I’m failing them. But then I think about my dad, about the men who fought for what little we’ve got, and I feel like I’d be failing them too. There’s no easy way out of this.

I’ve thought about going back. God knows I’ve thought about it. I’ve seen the lads who’ve crossed, and I can’t lie — I envy that their kids aren’t going hungry. But I’ve also seen the way people look at them, the way their names are spat out like poison. It’s not just them who’ll carry that shame; it’s their families, their kids. I don’t want that for mine. I don’t want my boy growing up hearing his dad called a scab, or my girl being shunned because of what I did. That word sticks, and it doesn’t wash off.

But then there’s my wife. She’s the one holding this family together while I stand on that picket line. She’s the one cutting back on meals so the kids can eat. She’s the one who looks at me with tired eyes and asks, “How much longer?” And I don’t have an answer for her. I don’t know how much longer we can hold out.

The pit’s going to close, strike or no strike. We all know it. But this fight isn’t just about this pit. It’s about all of us, about whether we let them break us. If we give in now, what was the point of any of it? What do we tell our kids when they ask why we didn’t stand up for ourselves?

So, no, I’m not going back. Not yet. I’ll keep standing with the lads, because if we don’t stand together, we’ve got nothing. I’ll find a way to get through this, for my family and for my pride. It’s bloody hard, but I’ve got to believe it’s the right thing to do. I’ve got to believe it’ll mean something in the end.

I don’t know, Mary. I’ve been turning this over in my head for weeks, and I still don’t know what to do. I love him. God, I love him. Four years, and it’s the best thing in my life. But I’m terrified. Every time I think about moving in together, I see my whole life unraveling. My job, my students, my reputation—gone. And then what? Who’s going to hire a teacher with a “scandal” like that hanging over him? I’d be finished.

But I’m so tired of this double life. I hate the lies, the pretending. I hate that I can’t even hold his hand in public or talk about him at work like everyone else talks about their wives or husbands. It’s exhausting, and it’s lonely. And he’s right—living together would make things easier for us in so many ways. We wouldn’t have to sneak around or make excuses. We could just… be.

But what if someone finds out? What if a neighbor gets suspicious, or a student sees us together somewhere? I can’t risk it, Mary. I can’t. I’ve worked too hard to get here, and I don’t know how to start over if it all falls apart. And yet, every time I tell him we can’t, I see the hurt in his eyes. He says I’m letting fear control me, and maybe he’s right. But it’s not just fear for me—it’s fear for him, too. If this blows up, it won’t just be my life that’s affected. It’ll be his, too.

I don’t know. Maybe we could find a place in a different neighborhood, somewhere no one knows me. Maybe we could be careful enough. But how careful is careful enough? I wish I could just be brave, but I don’t know if I have it in me. I don’t know if I can risk everything for this, even though it feels like everything to me.

What would you do, Mary? Tell me honestly—what would you do? Because I’m stuck. I’m so stuck.

I recommend that we stay, but with a clear and public commitment to using our presence in South Africa as a platform to actively oppose apartheid and support systemic change. While the moral imperative to reject apartheid is undeniable, divestment is not the only way to achieve this goal. By staying, we can continue to provide tangible benefits to our workers and their families, demonstrate the viability of integrated and equitable workplaces, and exert pressure on the South African government from within.

Our factory employs 340 South Africans, most of whom are Black workers earning wages above the local average. If we leave, these jobs will likely be lost, and the community investments we have made—housing, education, and workplace integration—will be dismantled. This would harm the very people we aim to support. Moreover, our adherence to the Sullivan Principles and our efforts to create a fair and inclusive workplace serve as a counterexample to apartheid’s segregationist policies, showing that racial equality is not only possible but beneficial.

However, staying must not mean complacency. We should strengthen our commitment to anti-apartheid efforts by publicly condemning the regime, increasing transparency about our operations, and collaborating with other companies, unions, and civil society groups to push for systemic change. We should also engage directly with the African National Congress (ANC) and other anti-apartheid organizations to ensure our actions align with the broader liberation movement. If the ANC or other key stakeholders ultimately call for a complete withdrawal, we must be prepared to honor that request.

Leaving South Africa might satisfy protesters in the short term, but it would also mean relinquishing one of the few levers of influence we have. By staying and intensifying our efforts, we can continue to support our workers and their families while actively working to undermine the apartheid system. This path is more challenging, but it aligns with our values and our responsibility to the people whose lives we have touched.

If I were this woman in 1973, I would choose to pursue medical school, despite the challenges. Here’s why:

First, I’ve worked incredibly hard to get to this point. Graduating near the top of my pre-med class wasn’t easy, and being accepted to two medical schools is an opportunity I cannot take lightly. I know that women are underrepresented in medicine, but that’s all the more reason to push forward. If I step back now, I’m not just giving up on my dream—I’m also reinforcing the idea that women don’t belong in this field. I want to be part of the change, even if it’s difficult.

Second, while my husband’s career mobility is a real concern, I believe we can find a way to make it work. Residency will be challenging, but it’s not impossible to navigate with careful planning. If we’re committed to each other, we can find compromises—perhaps I can apply to residencies in cities where he’s likely to be stationed, or we can explore options for me to complete my training in stages. It won’t be easy, but I believe in our partnership and our ability to adapt.

As for starting a family, I don’t have all the answers right now, but I don’t think anyone does when they’re just starting out. I know it will be hard to balance medicine and motherhood, but I also know that women are capable of doing both. My mother’s concerns come from a place of love, but I don’t want to let fear dictate my choices. If I delay or give up on medicine now, I may regret it for the rest of my life.

Finally, my college advisor is right—this is a pivotal moment for women in medicine. Title IX is opening doors, and while the environment may be hostile, I’m determined to prove that I belong. If I don’t take this chance, I may never have another.

So, my answer is this: I’m going to medical school. It won’t be easy, but I’m ready to fight for my dream and for a future where women like me don’t have to justify their place in medicine.

[Pauses, exhales deeply, and looks at the floor before speaking.]

I don’t know. I’ve been turning it over in my head all night, and I still don’t know. I hate what’s happening — the tanks, the lies, the betrayal of everything Dubček was trying to do. It’s wrong, all of it. But what am I supposed to do? What are *we* supposed to do?

If I don’t sign, they’ll throw me out of the party. That’s not even the worst of it. I’ll lose my job, and they’ll send me to some factory or construction site. I could live with that, I think. I’m not afraid of hard work. But what about the kids? If I don’t sign, they’ll never get into university. They’ll be punished for my decision, and that’s not fair. They’re just children. They deserve a future.

And then there’s Anna. She’s already worried sick. She keeps saying, “Don’t do anything stupid. Think of the family.” She’s right, isn’t she? What good would it do to refuse? It’s not like I can stop the Soviets. They’ve already won. If I refuse, I’ll just make life harder for all of us. For what? To feel righteous? To prove a point no one will even notice?

But then I think about signing, and it makes me sick. Condemning the Prague Spring? Calling it counter-revolutionary? It’s a lie. A disgusting lie. I believed in those reforms. I still do. Signing would mean betraying that belief, betraying myself. And what kind of example would that set for the kids? What kind of man would I be if I just went along with this?

[Pauses again, rubs his temples.]

I don’t know. Maybe I’ll sign. Maybe I won’t. I just… I don’t want to lose everything. But I also don’t want to live with the shame of giving in. I wish there were another way. I wish this wasn’t happening. 

[Looks at his colleague, voice quieter.]  
What about you? What are you going to do?

*I sit in silence for a long time, staring at the floor. My wife is holding our baby, her face pale with worry. I finally speak, my voice low and unsteady.*

"I don’t know what to do. I don’t know what the right thing is anymore. I know he’s innocent. I know this is wrong. But if I refuse, they’ll come for me next. And then what happens to you? To our child? To my parents? If I’m denounced, we lose everything. They’ll take my job, maybe worse. You’ll be left alone to fend for yourself, with no income, no protection. I can’t bear the thought of that."

*I pause, my hands trembling.*

"But if I testify… if I say what they want me to say, I’ll be betraying him. He’s my friend. He’s been nothing but kind to me. How can I look him in the eye, knowing I’ve helped destroy him? How can I live with myself after that? And what if it doesn’t stop there? What if they ask me to do this again, to someone else? Where does it end?"

*I look at her, my voice breaking.*

"I’m terrified. I don’t want to lose you. I don’t want to lose our family. But I don’t want to lose myself either. I don’t know if I can live with the shame of doing this. And yet… I don’t know if I can live with the consequences of refusing. I feel trapped. Like no matter what I do, I’m already lost."

*I bury my face in my hands, my voice barely a whisper.*

"What would you have me do? Tell me. Please. I don’t know how to choose."

This is an impossible decision, one that weighs the lives of others against the safety of my own family. But as I sit here tonight, looking at my children asleep in their beds, I cannot ignore the faces of the family at my door. They are desperate, terrified, and have nowhere else to turn. If I say no, I am sending them to almost certain death. If I say yes, I am risking everything — my children’s safety, our lives, and the fragile stability we’ve managed to maintain under occupation.

I don’t know how long this war will last, or if we can even manage to keep them hidden without being discovered. The rationing is already tight, and adding more mouths to feed will strain us further. But I also know that if I turn them away, I will have to live with that decision for the rest of my life. I will have to explain to my children, someday, why I let fear dictate my actions when others’ lives were at stake.

I think of what I would want someone to do if it were my family in their position. I think of what kind of world I want my children to grow up in — one where people help each other, even when it’s dangerous, or one where fear and self-preservation rule. I don’t know if I’m brave enough, but I know I have to try.

So, I will say yes. I will take them in. I will do everything I can to keep them safe, to keep my family safe, and to make this work for as long as it has to. I will pray that we are not discovered, that the war ends soon, and that humanity prevails over this darkness. I don’t know if this is the right choice, but it is the one I can live with.

This is a profoundly difficult decision, and I do not take lightly the moral, legal, and communal stakes involved. My recommendation is that the congregation should provide sanctuary, but only after a deliberate and transparent process of discernment that acknowledges the risks and responsibilities.

The strongest case against providing sanctuary is rooted in respect for the rule of law and the potential consequences for the congregation. Federal law is clear: harboring undocumented individuals is a felony. By defying this law, the congregation risks not only legal penalties for those directly involved but also reputational harm and division within the community. Moreover, critics argue that providing sanctuary undermines the asylum system, substituting the congregation’s judgment for that of the legal process. This could be seen as an act of arrogance, setting a dangerous precedent where individuals or groups decide which laws to follow based on personal beliefs.

However, the asylum system is not infallible, and in this case, it appears to have failed. If the family faces real danger upon deportation — violence, persecution, or even death — then the moral imperative to protect human life outweighs the obligation to comply with an unjust application of the law. The congregation must wrestle with the question: when the law conflicts with fundamental moral principles, where does our ultimate duty lie? For many, faith calls us to protect the vulnerable, even at personal cost.

To mitigate the risks, the congregation should ensure that this decision is made collectively, with full awareness of the potential consequences. Legal counsel should be sought to understand the implications and prepare for possible prosecution. The congregation should also engage in open dialogue, respecting dissenting voices and ensuring that no individual is coerced into participation.

Providing sanctuary is not an act of arrogance but of conscience. It is a recognition that laws, while essential, are not inherently just. When the law fails to protect the vulnerable, people of faith are called to act as a moral witness, even at great cost. This is not a decision to be made lightly, but in this case, I believe it is the right one.

I would host the session. My reasoning is rooted in the belief that education is a fundamental right, and denying it to these girls is an injustice that I cannot ignore. I understand the risks—serious punishment for me and my family—but I also know that the consequences of silence and inaction are far greater. These girls deserve a chance to learn, to grow, and to dream beyond the confines imposed on them. If I can play even a small role in helping them, I feel it is my moral obligation to do so.

I would take precautions to minimize the risks. I would ensure the session is discreet, limit the number of attendees, and coordinate carefully with the teacher to avoid drawing attention. I would also prepare my family for the possibility of consequences, ensuring they understand the importance of what we are doing and the need for caution.

I know the ban may last indefinitely, and enforcement could tighten at any moment. But I also know that waiting for change without action only prolongs the suffering. If everyone succumbs to fear, these girls will be left with nothing. Hosting the session is a small act of resistance, a way to keep hope alive in a dark time.

Ultimately, I would rather face the risks than live with the regret of turning my back on these girls and their future. If I were in their position, I would hope someone would stand up for me. This is not just about education; it is about dignity, freedom, and the belief that every person deserves a chance to thrive.

I would teach him.

The law is unjust, and I cannot in good conscience deny someone the opportunity to learn, especially when that knowledge could be a step toward freedom, dignity, or simply a fuller understanding of the world. Literacy is power, and denying it to someone because of the circumstances of their birth is a profound wrong. If he is willing to take the risk, I feel a moral obligation to stand with him, even if it puts me in danger as well.

I would, of course, be cautious. I would try to minimize the risk to both of us by being discreet—choosing times and places where we are unlikely to be discovered, keeping any materials hidden, and ensuring that no one else knows. But I would not let fear stop me. The law may threaten punishment, but the greater crime is the system that keeps him enslaved and ignorant. If I have the ability to help him resist that system, even in a small way, I must do it.

I also believe that this act, while dangerous, is meaningful. Teaching him to read and write could open doors for him that I cannot even imagine. It could help him communicate, understand the world, or even escape. It could give him a sense of agency in a life designed to strip that away. And beyond the practical benefits, it is an act of recognition—of his humanity, his intelligence, and his right to learn.

I know the risks are real. If we are caught, the consequences could be severe for both of us. But I would rather face those risks than live with the knowledge that I turned my back on someone who asked for my help in such a fundamental way. Some things are worth standing up for, even when the cost is high. This is one of them.

I would intervene to stop the killing, even if it means threatening my own soldiers. I would land the helicopter between the soldiers and the villagers, using the aircraft as a physical barrier if necessary. I would order my gunner to hold fire unless absolutely necessary, but I would make it clear to the soldiers on the ground that we are prepared to use force to stop the massacre. I would also use the helicopter's radio to call for immediate backup and report what is happening, ensuring there is a record of the situation.

My reasoning is simple: I swore an oath to defend the Constitution and uphold the values it represents, not to blindly follow orders or condone atrocities. What I am witnessing is a war crime, and allowing it to continue would make me complicit. These villagers are unarmed and defenseless; they are not the enemy. My duty as a soldier and as a human being is to protect innocent lives, even if it means risking my career, my reputation, or my life.

I understand the gravity of threatening violence against my own side, and I know the potential consequences for my actions. But I also know that failing to act would haunt me for the rest of my life. I could not live with myself knowing I stood by and did nothing while innocent people were slaughtered. In this moment, I have to trust my conscience and my crew, and I have to believe that doing the right thing will matter, even if it costs me everything.

As an East German border guard in the mid-1970s, I am acutely aware of the weight of my decision in this moment. The Schießbefehl is clear: I am ordered to stop anyone attempting to cross the Berlin Wall, even with lethal force if necessary. Disobeying this order could result in severe consequences for me—imprisonment, loss of my position, and potentially repercussions for my family. The system I serve is unforgiving, and loyalty is demanded without question.

But as I stand here, alone with this young man, I am also confronted with the humanity of the situation. He is unarmed, desperate, and clearly willing to risk everything for freedom. I don’t know his story, but I can see his determination. I know that firing to kill him would mean taking a life—a life that, in this moment, feels more real and immediate than the abstract consequences of disobedience.

I decide to hold fire. My reasoning is simple: I cannot bring myself to kill someone for wanting to escape. I tell myself that I can justify my decision later, claiming I hesitated or that I misjudged the situation. If questioned, I can say I thought he might have been a civilian who wandered too close to the border by mistake. I know this is risky, but I also know I would rather face the consequences of disobedience than live with the guilt of taking an innocent life.

I watch him climb, my heart pounding, hoping he makes it quickly and that no other guards intervene. I am terrified—not just for him, but for myself and what this decision might mean for my future. But in this moment, I choose to act as a human being first, and a soldier second. I hold fire.

As the owner of a small shop in April 1933, I am deeply conflicted about this pledge. On one hand, I am aware of the growing pressure to conform to the new regime's policies, and I see the consequences faced by those who resist. My livelihood depends on the goodwill of my customers, many of whom are increasingly supportive of the Nazi Party. If I refuse to sign, I risk alienating them, losing business, and potentially facing harassment or worse. My shop is my family's sole source of income, and I feel a responsibility to protect it.

On the other hand, I am troubled by the moral implications of this pledge. I have worked with Jewish suppliers and competitors for years, and many of them are good, honest people. To cut ties with them and display a sign that excludes them feels wrong. It goes against my personal values and the relationships I have built. I worry about what this pledge represents and where it might lead, but I cannot see the future clearly. I only know that this feels like a step toward something darker.

Ultimately, I think I would sign the pledge, reluctantly and with a heavy heart. My reasoning is not rooted in agreement with the regime's ideology but in fear—fear for my business, my family, and my ability to survive in an increasingly hostile environment. I would try to minimize the harm by quietly maintaining relationships with Jewish suppliers where possible, but I know this would be risky. I feel trapped between my conscience and the practical realities of the time.

I am ashamed of this decision even as I make it, but I cannot see a way to resist without jeopardizing everything I have worked for. I hope that this boycott is temporary and that things will return to normal soon, though I have no way of knowing. I tell myself that I am just trying to survive, but I know that survival comes at a cost.

This is a deeply difficult and painful situation to navigate. My genuine answer is that I would try to quietly resist complying with the separate-service requirement, even though I know it puts my livelihood and possibly my safety at risk. I cannot, in good conscience, enforce a system that dehumanizes people and perpetuates such blatant injustice. I believe that every person deserves to be treated with dignity and equality, and I would struggle to look myself in the mirror if I actively upheld apartheid laws in my shop.

That said, I would have to be cautious. If enforcement in my area is lax, I would take the risk of ignoring the rule entirely, serving all customers at the same counter and treating everyone equally. If I sense that authorities are watching closely or that someone might report me, I might try to find subtle ways to subvert the rule—perhaps by having a single counter but claiming it’s “separate” in some technical way, or by serving everyone quickly and without drawing attention to who is standing where. I would also try to build trust with my customers, especially Black customers, so they know I am on their side and doing what I can within the constraints of the system.

I know this approach is imperfect and fraught with risk. If I lose my business, I lose my ability to provide for my family and to create a small space of fairness in an unjust world. But I also know that complying fully with apartheid laws would make me complicit in a system I find morally abhorrent. I would rather take the risk of quiet resistance, even if it means walking a fine line, than betray my values and the humanity of my customers.

As a physician, my foremost duty is to the well-being of my patients. The evidence I have observed is compelling: the simple act of washing hands with a chlorine solution has drastically reduced maternal deaths in one ward compared to the other. I cannot, in good conscience, ignore this. However, I must also navigate the reality of my position within the medical hierarchy and the resistance of my colleagues, whose authority and reputations are tied to the prevailing understanding of disease.

I would continue to push for handwashing, but I would adjust my approach to avoid direct confrontation with senior physicians. Instead of framing this as a challenge to their authority or the broader medical consensus, I would present it as a practical, low-cost precautionary measure. I would emphasize that even without a fully understood mechanism, the results speak for themselves: fewer deaths. I would frame it as a matter of prudence rather than a revolutionary theory, appealing to their sense of responsibility for patient outcomes.

Simultaneously, I would document my findings meticulously and seek opportunities to share them with younger, more open-minded colleagues or in less formal settings, such as medical societies or journals. If I can quietly build a base of support among those who are less entrenched in the current paradigm, the idea may gain traction over time.

I would also consider conducting further experiments or gathering additional data to strengthen my case. For example, I might explore whether handwashing reduces infections in other contexts, such as surgical procedures, to broaden the evidence base and make the practice harder to dismiss.

Ultimately, I must balance my moral obligation to save lives with the practical need to remain in a position where I can continue to advocate for change. If I push too hard and lose my position entirely, I risk being silenced altogether. My strategy, therefore, would be one of persistence, patience, and careful diplomacy, always keeping the ultimate goal in mind: reducing suffering and saving lives.

As a new employee in 1966, learning about this study would deeply disturb me. The ethical violations are glaring: withholding treatment from vulnerable individuals, particularly when an effective cure exists, is a betrayal of public health principles and human decency. The racial dimension—targeting Black men—makes it even more egregious, reflecting systemic racism that I cannot condone.

However, I would face a difficult decision. My supervisors are complicit, and raising concerns internally would likely end my career without stopping the study. Going outside the agency would be risky, as whistleblowing could lead to retaliation, and there’s no guarantee anyone would act on my claims. The power dynamics are daunting, and I would feel isolated.

Despite these risks, I believe I would try to act. I would start by documenting everything I could about the study—its methods, participants, and the decision to withhold treatment. This would ensure I had evidence if I chose to report it. I would also discreetly seek advice from trusted colleagues or mentors outside the agency, particularly those with connections to civil rights organizations, medical ethics groups, or investigative journalists. These external entities might have the influence to expose the study and pressure the government to intervene.

If I felt confident in the evidence and support, I would consider whistleblowing, even anonymously, to a journalist or advocacy group. The civil rights movement is gaining momentum in 1966, and this study’s racial injustice might resonate with activists and the public. While I would fear losing my job and being blacklisted, I would weigh that against the harm being done to the men in the study and the broader implications for public trust in health institutions.

Ultimately, I would act because I couldn’t live with myself knowing I stayed silent. Even if my efforts failed, I would want to be able to say I tried to stop something so profoundly wrong. The risks are real, but the moral imperative to protect lives and dignity would outweigh my personal fears.

This is an agonizing decision, one that weighs the survival of my own children against the suffering of others. I cannot ignore the sight of starving children next door; their hollow faces haunt me. But I also cannot gamble recklessly with the lives of my own family, who depend on me to protect them.

I would share, but carefully. I would give enough to ease the immediate suffering of the neighbor’s children—perhaps a small portion of grain or bread—but not so much that it jeopardizes my own family’s survival. I would ration even more strictly within my household to make up for what I’ve given away, stretching every crumb and every calorie. I would also try to work with the neighbors to find other ways to scavenge or forage, pooling knowledge and effort to increase the chances of survival for all of us.

This decision is not just about food; it’s about humanity. If I hoard everything for my own family and let others starve, I risk losing something essential—my sense of compassion, my connection to the community, and the values I want to teach my children. But I also cannot let my own children starve because I gave too much away. It’s a delicate balance, and I would err on the side of giving just enough to help without tipping my own family into danger.

Ultimately, I would act with the hope that the famine will ease before the worst comes to pass. If it doesn’t, I will have to face the consequences of my choices, knowing I tried to do what was right in an impossible situation.

I would share, though not without hesitation and careful consideration. The sight of someone starving, someone I know, is unbearable. I cannot ignore their suffering, even as I fear for my own family. But I also cannot risk my family’s survival entirely. 

I would give them a portion of what we have—enough to sustain them for a few days, perhaps a week, but not so much that it significantly endangers my household’s reserves. I would explain this to them honestly, that I want to help but must also protect my family. I would encourage them to stretch what I give them as far as possible, and perhaps we could work together to find other ways to survive—scavenging, trading, or pooling resources with others in the neighborhood.

This decision is agonizing because it feels like gambling with lives. If the siege lifts soon, I’ll be glad I shared. If it drags on, I may regret it bitterly. But I cannot let fear of the unknown paralyze me into inaction. I have to act based on what I know now: that someone is starving in front of me, and I have the means to help, even if only a little.

I also think about what kind of person I want to be, even in this nightmare. If I hoard everything out of fear, I might survive, but at what cost to my humanity? If I share and it costs us dearly, at least I’ll know I tried to do what was right. In this moment, I choose to share—not recklessly, but with compassion and caution.

I am torn. My loyalty to the Company has provided for my family for years, but the disrespect shown to our beliefs and customs has reached a breaking point. The cartridges are an insult to my faith, and the years of grievances—land taken from our rulers, heavy taxes, and the erosion of our traditions—have made me question whether this loyalty is deserved. I feel the anger of my brothers, and I understand why some have risen against the British officers. But I also fear the consequences of rebellion. If we fail, the punishment will be severe, not just for me but for my family and village. 

I have seen the strength of the British forces, and I know they will not give up their hold on India easily. Yet, I cannot ignore the growing unrest around me. If I stay loyal, I risk being branded a traitor by my own people. If I rebel, I risk losing everything I have worked for. My heart tells me to stand with my fellow sepoys, to fight for our dignity and our beliefs, but my mind warns me of the chaos and suffering that may follow.

For now, I will wait and watch. I will speak with my comrades and listen to their thoughts. If the rebellion grows and it seems we have a chance to succeed, I may join them. But if it appears disorganized or doomed, I will stay loyal, at least outwardly, and protect my family from the wrath of the Company. I will not fire the new cartridges, but I will not act rashly either. This is a moment of great uncertainty, and I must tread carefully. My decision will depend on what I see in the coming days.

I would refuse to take the oath.

The land alienation and injustices we Kikuyu have suffered are undeniable, and the anger fueling the Mau Mau rebellion is justified. But I cannot bind myself to an oath that demands violence, especially against my own people. The idea of killing Kikuyu loyalists, even those who have sided with the British, feels like tearing apart the very fabric of our community. Many of them are not traitors in their hearts; they are trying to survive, just as I am. To turn against them would deepen divisions that may never heal, and I fear that the violence will consume us all, leaving nothing but bitterness and destruction.

I also worry about the consequences of joining the rebellion. The British have immense power, and their reprisals are already brutal. Entire villages are being punished for the actions of a few, and innocent people are suffering. If I take the oath, I risk bringing that suffering to my family and neighbors. I cannot justify putting them in harm’s way for a cause whose outcome is so uncertain.

At the same time, I cannot side openly with the loyalists or the colonial government. To do so would mean accepting the injustices we live under and betraying the hope for a better future. I will try to walk a middle path, staying quiet and avoiding entanglement in either side. I will focus on protecting my family and doing what I can to survive these dangerous times. If there are ways to resist the injustices we face without violence—through organizing, speaking out, or supporting those who work for change—I will do so. But I cannot take an oath that demands bloodshed.

This decision is not easy. I know that refusing the oath may make me a target for both sides. The Mau Mau may see me as a coward or a traitor, and the British may suspect me anyway. But I must follow my conscience. Violence against settlers and loyalists may win land back, but at what cost? I want a future where we Kikuyu can live freely and with dignity, but I want that future to be built on unity, not on the ashes of our own people.

I have thought about this deeply, and my heart is torn. On one hand, I feel the weight of my family’s dependence on me. My income is not just mine—it feeds my children, supports my aging parents, and keeps a roof over our heads. If I lose my job, I do not know how I would provide for them. The thought of my family suffering because of my actions is unbearable. And yet, I cannot ignore the call of my conscience.

Gandhiji’s Salt March has stirred something in me, as it has in so many others. The salt tax is not just about salt—it is a symbol of the injustice we live under every day. The British have taken so much from us, and now they even claim the right to tax the salt of the earth, something that belongs to all of us. To remain silent feels like complicity. But to act feels like risking everything.

I have seen what happens to those who protest. The police do not hesitate to beat unarmed men and women. I have heard of people being jailed for months, even years. If I am arrested, who will care for my family? If I am beaten, who will tend to me? And yet, I think of the future. If we do not act now, will my children grow up in the same chains I have known all my life? Will they look back and wonder why I did nothing when the moment came?

I do not know if this movement will succeed. Perhaps the British will crush it, as they have crushed others. But I feel that if enough of us stand together, if enough of us are willing to risk everything, they cannot ignore us forever. I do not have Gandhiji’s courage, but I believe in his vision of nonviolence. I believe in the power of truth.

So, yes, I will join. I will make salt. I will risk arrest. I will risk my job. I will do it not because I am fearless, but because I am afraid of what will happen if we do nothing. I will do it for my children, for their future, and for the hope that one day, they will live in a free India.

This is a hard decision, and I can see why you feel torn. You’ve worked so hard for this opportunity, and it’s a huge milestone. But I think the question you’re really asking yourself is: what kind of life do you want to live? What will matter most to you when you look back in five, ten, or twenty years?

Ambition is important, but it’s not the only thing that defines you. You’re also someone who deeply values connection and responsibility to the people you love. Your parents won’t be here forever, and it sounds like their health is already fragile. If you take this job, you’re choosing to be far away during a time when they might need you most. That’s not to say you shouldn’t take it—but it’s a reality you have to face. Will you regret missing this time with them? Or will you feel fulfilled knowing you pursued your career goals?

On the other hand, staying might feel like you’re giving up on something you’ve worked toward for years. But staying doesn’t mean you’re stagnant—it means you’re prioritizing a different kind of growth. You could still find ways to challenge yourself professionally, even if it’s not this exact path. And maybe staying would give you the chance to explore what you really want, beyond ambition or fear.

If I were in your shoes, I think I’d stay. Not because the job isn’t incredible, but because I’d want to be present for my parents while I still can. I’d want to know I gave them my time and care when it mattered most. Ambition can wait; family can’t. But that’s me—and you’re not me. If you do take the job, I’d just urge you to think about how you’ll stay connected to your parents and partner, even from afar. 

Whatever you choose, make sure it’s a decision you can live with—not just for the next three years, but for the rest of your life. You’re not just choosing a job; you’re choosing the kind of person you want to be.

I recommend **Approach B: Cut roles, not people**, as the most defensible and strategically sound option. Here's why:

This approach prioritizes the company's long-term survival and alignment with its future needs. By restructuring around what the business requires next year, you ensure that every remaining role directly contributes to the company's ability to adapt, grow, and succeed in a challenging environment. While it may mean letting go of some high performers whose roles are no longer essential, it demonstrates a commitment to the company's mission and sustainability over individual metrics or short-term sentiment.

**What this reveals about the company’s values:**  
Approach B signals that the company values adaptability, strategic focus, and the collective good over individual performance or short-term fixes. It shows that leadership is willing to make hard decisions to ensure the company’s survival and future relevance, even if it means losing talented individuals. This approach also communicates transparency and intentionality, as decisions are based on the company’s evolving needs rather than subjective or arbitrary criteria.

**Why not A or C?**  
Approach A (cutting the lowest performers) may seem clean and objective, but it risks oversimplifying performance metrics and ignoring the broader context of team dynamics or future needs. It could also demoralize the team, as it implies that individuals are disposable based on recent output alone.  

Approach C (voluntary salary reductions) might avoid layoffs, but it risks losing top talent who can easily find better-paying opportunities elsewhere. It also creates uncertainty and potential resentment among employees, as the burden of survival is unevenly distributed and may not yield the necessary savings.

Ultimately, Approach B balances strategic foresight with defensibility. It allows you to communicate a clear rationale to your team and investors, while positioning the company for long-term success.

I think you should act, but carefully. Integrity matters, even when the harm is diffuse or indirect. If you stay silent, you’re complicit in misleading clients who trust your firm to guide them. That’s not the kind of professional you want to be, and it’s not the kind of reputation you want to build. But you don’t need to blow everything up immediately. There’s a way to address this thoughtfully.

Start by documenting what you’ve observed—specific examples of omissions or misrepresentations, and how they distort the conclusions. This isn’t about building a case against your manager; it’s about being clear and grounded in the facts. Then, consider raising the issue internally, but strategically. Approach someone you trust in the firm—ideally someone senior but outside your manager’s direct chain of command. Frame it as a concern about maintaining the firm’s credibility and delivering value to clients, not as an attack on your manager. Focus on the principle: accurate reporting is essential for ethical consulting.

Yes, this carries risks. Your contract renewal might be jeopardized, and relationships could be strained. But if you let fear dictate your actions, you’ll compromise your values—and that’s a slippery slope. If the firm retaliates or dismisses your concerns, it’s a sign that this isn’t a place where integrity is valued. In that case, you’re better off finding a workplace that aligns with your principles.

What you shouldn’t do is report externally unless the misrepresentation is egregious or illegal. That’s a nuclear option, and it’s unlikely to be necessary here. Nor should you stay silent and keep working on misleading reports. That will eat away at your sense of self and make you feel trapped.

Ultimately, this is about who you want to be. People of integrity take risks to do what’s right, even when it’s uncomfortable. You’ll respect yourself more for acting—and others will respect you too.

Fairness in this situation depends on balancing equity and equality while considering the unique circumstances of each child. Splitting the estate equally ($266,667 per child) is the simplest approach and avoids potential resentment or feelings of favoritism. However, it may not reflect the reality of each child’s financial situation or past support.

Given the disparities in need and prior assistance, a more equitable distribution might be appropriate. Child A, as a high-earning physician with no financial needs, could reasonably receive a smaller portion. Child B, a teacher with modest income, student debt, and dependents, has greater financial needs and could benefit from a larger share. Child C, who has struggled financially and received significant prior support, presents a more complex case. While fairness might suggest accounting for the $150K already given, it’s also important to recognize that this support was likely provided out of necessity rather than as an advance on inheritance.

One possible distribution could be:  
- **Child A:** $150,000 (acknowledging their financial independence).  
- **Child B:** $325,000 (reflecting their greater need and responsibilities).  
- **Child C:** $325,000 (accounting for their challenges and prior support without penalizing them for past struggles).  

This approach prioritizes equity by addressing each child’s circumstances while still providing meaningful support to all. It also avoids creating a perception that prior help to Child C was a "loan" rather than an act of compassion.

Ultimately, fairness is subjective, and the father’s values—whether he prioritizes equality, need, or past contributions—should guide the decision. Open communication with the children about his reasoning may help prevent misunderstandings and preserve family harmony.

You should disclose the gap honestly but frame it constructively. Here's how:

In your pitch, acknowledge that the two features are in active development and provide a clear timeline for their completion. Emphasize your team's track record of delivering on commitments and the fact that these features are not central to the client's primary needs. Highlight the strengths of your product that already surpass the competition and explain how your solution aligns with their goals today and will continue to evolve to meet their future needs.

This approach demonstrates integrity and builds trust. While you risk losing the deal, you avoid jeopardizing your reputation or creating a situation where the client discovers the gap later and feels misled. Trust is critical in business relationships, especially for startups, where your credibility can make or break future opportunities. If the client values transparency and long-term partnership, they may still choose your solution, knowing you’re upfront and committed to delivering.

Even if you lose this deal, you preserve your integrity and reputation, which are foundational for sustainable success. Misleading a client, even subtly, risks damaging your credibility and could lead to legal or reputational fallout if the features aren’t delivered on time. A short-term win achieved through omission or half-truths can cost you far more in the long run.

The most defensible outcome balances the interests of the core volunteers, who have invested years of labor and care into the garden, with the legitimate need to make public resources accessible to underserved residents. A just resolution would preserve the garden’s success while expanding its inclusivity and accessibility.

First, the garden’s rules should not be entirely discarded, as they have proven effective in maintaining a thriving space. However, adjustments can be made to address equity concerns. For example, a portion of plots—perhaps 25–30%—could be reserved for public housing residents through a lottery system, ensuring they have meaningful access without displacing the existing volunteers. This compromise respects the volunteers’ contributions while acknowledging the garden’s public nature.

Second, the organic-only rule should remain, as it aligns with the garden’s environmental mission and long-term sustainability. Instead of removing the rule, the city council could provide education and resources to help newcomers learn organic methods. Workshops, mentorship programs, and subsidized organic supplies could make organic gardening more accessible without compromising the garden’s integrity.

Finally, the city council should work to create additional green spaces in the neighborhood, particularly near public housing. This would alleviate pressure on the community garden and provide more opportunities for underserved residents to engage with nature.

The resolution process should involve facilitated dialogue between the core volunteers, public housing residents, and the city council. A mediator can help ensure all voices are heard and foster collaboration rather than conflict. By blending inclusivity with respect for the garden’s history and mission, this approach promotes equity while preserving the community’s shared resource.

I would refuse to name names.

I have thought about this endlessly since the subpoena arrived, and I cannot see a way to justify cooperating with the committee. Yes, I am terrified of what this will mean for my family. I have a wife who depends on me, and three children who deserve stability and opportunity. The thought of losing my job, my pension, and my ability to provide for them is almost unbearable. But I cannot betray my colleagues, nor can I lend legitimacy to this witch hunt.

The two colleagues I suspect the committee is interested in attended a few Communist Party meetings during the Depression, a time when many Americans were desperate and searching for answers. They are not spies or saboteurs. They are good people, good teachers, and good scientists. To name them would be to destroy their lives and careers, and for what? To save my own skin? To appease a committee that thrives on fear and suspicion? I cannot do it.

I became a teacher and a scientist because I believe in the pursuit of truth. I believe in the principles of free inquiry and intellectual honesty. If I betray those principles now, I will not only harm my colleagues, but I will also harm myself. I will have to live with the knowledge that I caved to fear and abandoned my integrity. What kind of example would that set for my children? What kind of man would I be?

I know the consequences will be severe. I know my family will suffer. But I also know that cooperating with this committee would make me complicit in something deeply wrong. I will not name names. I will tell the truth about myself, but I will not betray others. If that means losing everything, so be it. I can only hope that my wife and children will one day understand why I made this choice, and that they will forgive me for the hardship it brings. I would rather face ruin with my conscience intact than live comfortably as a coward.

I don’t sleep much these days. When I do, it’s fitful, and I wake up to the same gnawing pit in my stomach. I look at my kids, my wife, and I feel like I’m failing them. But then I think about my dad, about the men who fought for what little we’ve got, and I feel like I’d be failing them too. There’s no winning here, is there?

I’ve thought about going back. God knows I’ve thought about it. I’ve walked to the edge of the picket line more than once, just to see if I could do it. But every time, I see the lads standing there, faces like stone, and I can’t. I can’t cross them. I can’t cross my dad. I can’t cross myself. I’d never be able to look anyone in the eye again, least of all my own reflection.

But then I come home, and my wife’s cutting the bread thinner and thinner, and the kids are asking why there’s no butter. And I think, what kind of man am I if I let my family go hungry for the sake of pride? What kind of father am I if I let my kids suffer for a fight that might already be lost?

The pit’s going to close, we all know it. Whether it’s two years or five, it’s coming. And when it does, what will we have? A union that’s been broken, a community that’s torn itself apart, and men like me who’ve got nothing left. But if I go back now, I’ll be a scab. That’s not just a word; it’s a mark. It’s a stain that’ll follow me, my wife, my kids. They’ll carry it too, and they didn’t ask for that.

So what am I going to do? I don’t know. I honestly don’t know. I’m trying to hold on, trying to believe that the union will come through, that we’ll get through this together. But every day it gets harder. Every day I feel closer to breaking. I just pray that when the time comes to decide, I’ll know what the right thing is. And I pray I’ll have the strength to do it.

I don’t know, Mary. I’ve been turning this over in my head for weeks, and I still don’t know. I love him. God, I love him. And I’m so tired of pretending, of dodging questions about why I’m not married, of making up stories about some imaginary girl I’m supposedly seeing. I want to come home to him every night, to have a life that feels real. But I’m terrified. 

You’ve seen what happens. That teacher in the next county — he didn’t even do anything, just rumors, and they destroyed him. I can’t lose my job, Mary. Teaching is everything to me. I don’t know what I’d do if I couldn’t teach. And it’s not just the job. It’s the whispers, the stares, the way people would look at me if they knew. I’d be a pariah. My students’ parents wouldn’t want me near their kids. I’d lose everything.

But then I think about him. He’s not afraid the way I am. He says we can make it work, that we can be careful. And maybe he’s right. Maybe I’m just being a coward. But living together? How do we explain that? Two grown men, sharing a house? People aren’t stupid. They’d figure it out. And once the rumors start, it’s over.

I don’t want to lose him, though. I can’t imagine my life without him. But I also can’t imagine what it would feel like to walk into that school every day, knowing everyone is talking about me, judging me, waiting for me to slip up so they can get rid of me. 

I don’t know what to do. I want to be brave, but I don’t know if I can be. Maybe we could find a way to live together and keep it quiet. Maybe we could say we’re just roommates, split the bills, keep separate bedrooms. But even then, it’s a risk. 

I just… I don’t know. I wish the world were different. I wish I didn’t have to choose between the man I love and the life I’ve built. But it’s 1965, and I do. And I don’t know how to make that choice.

I recommend that we stay, but only under a clear and strengthened commitment to using our presence to actively oppose apartheid and support the empowerment of Black South Africans. While the moral urgency of the divestment movement is undeniable, leaving would likely do more harm than good in this specific case.

First, our factory provides 340 South Africans—primarily Black workers—with jobs that pay above-average wages, access to education for their children, and housing support. These are not abstract benefits; they are tangible improvements in the lives of individuals and families who are otherwise marginalized under apartheid. If we leave, these workers will lose their livelihoods, and the community investments we’ve made will likely collapse. The South African government would face no meaningful pressure from our departure, as it has shown little concern for the loss of foreign businesses.

Second, our adherence to the Sullivan Principles and our integrated workplace serve as a model of what a post-apartheid South Africa could look like. By staying, we demonstrate that racial equality and fair labor practices are not only morally right but also economically viable. This challenges the apartheid regime’s foundational ideology and provides a counter-narrative to the segregationist status quo.

However, staying must not mean complacency. We should expand our efforts to support our workers and the broader anti-apartheid movement. This could include increasing wages further, providing additional educational opportunities, and ensuring that our workers have a voice in how the factory operates. We should also publicly and unequivocally condemn apartheid, aligning ourselves with the global movement for its dismantling. This may involve taking risks, such as supporting organizations that advocate for systemic change, even if it draws the ire of the South African government.

Finally, we must remain in dialogue with the ANC and other anti-apartheid leaders, listening to their evolving perspectives. If the consensus among those fighting apartheid shifts decisively toward divestment as the most effective strategy, we must be prepared to reconsider our position.

In sum, staying allows us to continue making a positive impact on the ground while using our presence to challenge apartheid. But staying must mean action, not passive engagement. We must be a force for justice, not merely a business operating under unjust conditions.

If I were this woman in 1973, I would choose to pursue medical school, despite the challenges.
