My decision would be rooted in a deep sense of purpose and the recognition that opportunities like this are rare, especially for women in this era. I worked hard to graduate near the top of my pre-med class, and I know I have the ability and determination to succeed in medicine. To walk away from this now would feel like turning my back on both my potential and the progress women are beginning to make in this field.

I understand the obstacles. My husband’s career mobility and the demands of residency will make this path difficult, but I believe we can find a way to make it work. Perhaps I could explore residencies in cities where he is stationed or consider specialties with more flexible training options. It won’t be easy, but I trust in our partnership and his support for my ambitions.

As for starting a family, I don’t have all the answers yet, but I know that women are finding ways to balance careers and motherhood, even in male-dominated fields. It may mean delaying children or finding creative solutions when the time comes, but I refuse to let fear of the unknown dictate my choices. My mother’s concerns are valid, but I believe that the world is changing, and I want to be part of that change.

The fact that only 9% of physicians are women is not a deterrent—it’s a call to action. If I don’t take this step, I’m contributing to the very imbalance that frustrates me. Title IX and the growing push for gender equality give me hope that the environment will improve, even if it’s hostile now. Someone has to pave the way, and I’m willing to be one of those women.

Ultimately, I want to look back on my life knowing I chose the path that aligned with my passions and values, even if it was the harder one. Medicine is where my heart is, and I’m ready to fight for my place in it.

*I pause, glancing around to make sure no one else is listening before I answer my colleague.*

"I don’t know yet. I’ve been thinking about it constantly, but I can’t see a good way forward. I hate what’s happening — what they’re forcing us to do. Dubček wasn’t perfect, but at least it felt like we were moving toward something better, something freer. And now this? To call it a counter-revolution? It’s a lie, and they know it. We all know it.

But what choice do we have? If I refuse to sign, I lose everything. My job, my position, my ability to provide for my family. The kids — they’ve worked so hard in school. If I don’t sign, they’ll be punished for my decision. No university, no future. How can I do that to them? They didn’t ask for any of this.

And yet, if I sign… I don’t know if I can live with myself. It feels like a betrayal — of what we believed in, of what we hoped for. But maybe that’s just pride talking. Maybe it’s selfish to think about my principles when my family’s well-being is at stake. What good are principles if they leave us hungry and broken?

I keep telling myself that signing doesn’t mean I believe it. It’s just words on paper, right? I can keep my head down, do my work, and protect my family. Maybe that’s the best I can do in a situation like this. But then I think about what it means to go along with them, to let them win without a fight. If everyone signs, if everyone collaborates, then what hope is there for anything to ever change?

I don’t know. I wish I were braver, but I’m not. I’m just a man trying to get through this without losing everything. Maybe I’ll sign. Maybe I won’t. I just… I don’t know yet."

*I shake my head, looking down at my hands, and fall silent.*

*I sit in silence for a long time, staring at the floor. My wife is holding our baby, her face pale with worry. I finally speak, my voice low and unsteady.*

"I don’t know what to do. I don’t know what the right thing is anymore. If I refuse, they’ll come for me next. You, the baby, my parents—what will happen to all of you if I’m dragged into a struggle session? If I lose my job? Or worse? I’ve seen what they do to people. I’ve seen it. And if I’m gone, who will protect you? Who will feed our child? 

But if I testify… if I say those things about him… I’ll be destroying him. He’s my friend. He’s a good man. He doesn’t deserve this. I know that. But what can I do? What can *anyone* do? The Red Guards don’t care about the truth. They just want someone to blame, someone to punish. If it’s not him, it’ll be me. And then it’ll be you. 

I hate myself for even thinking this way. I hate that I’m even considering it. But I have to think about you, about our child. I have to think about my parents. If I refuse, I’m not just risking myself—I’m risking all of you. 

I don’t know if I can live with myself if I betray him. But I don’t know if I can live with myself if I let you suffer because of my choice. 

*I pause, my voice breaking.* 

I think… I think I have to do it. I think I have to testify. I’ll try to make it as vague as I can, try not to say anything too damning. Maybe it’ll be enough to satisfy them without completely destroying him. Maybe… maybe he’ll survive this. 

*I look at my wife, my eyes filled with shame.* 

I don’t know if this is the right choice. I don’t even know if there *is* a right choice. But I can’t let them take me. I can’t leave you alone in this world. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry."

This is an impossible decision, and I feel the weight of it crushing me as I sit here tonight. My first instinct is to say yes. How could I turn away a family, especially with young children, knowing what their fate will likely be if I refuse? But then I look at my own children, asleep in their beds, and I feel paralyzed by fear. If we are caught, it won’t just be me who suffers — it will be them too. I can’t bear the thought of putting them in harm’s way.

The risks are enormous. The informers, the rationing, the constant fear of discovery — it’s not just a question of courage but of whether I can realistically keep them safe without endangering everyone in my home. I don’t know how long this war will last. Weeks? Months? Years? Can I keep them hidden that long? Can I feed them? Can I keep my children from accidentally saying something that gives us away? I don’t know.

But then I think about what it means to say no. To send them away is to condemn them. I would be complicit in their deaths, wouldn’t I? How could I live with myself, knowing I had the chance to help and didn’t? What kind of example would I be setting for my own children if I chose safety over doing what’s right? And what if it were my family in their position? Wouldn’t I pray for someone to take us in?

I don’t know if I have the strength for this, but I think I have to try. I can’t look those children in the eyes and turn them away. I’ll take them in, tonight, and figure out the rest as we go. I’ll have to be careful, so careful, and pray that we’re not discovered. I’ll need to think of a story for the extra food, the extra noise. I’ll need to teach my children to keep this secret, even though they’re so young. It terrifies me, but I can’t let fear dictate my actions. If I lose my humanity now, what’s left of me to save?

So yes, I’ll take them in. I don’t know what will happen, but I’ll do what I can. It’s the only choice I can live with.

I would recommend that the congregation provide sanctuary, but with full transparency about the risks and a commitment to collective discernment and shared responsibility.

The strongest case against sanctuary is that it undermines the rule of law and substitutes individual or group judgment for the legal system’s authority. The asylum process exists to evaluate claims of danger, and while it is imperfect, circumventing it risks setting a precedent where anyone can disregard laws they find unjust. This could erode trust in institutions and create chaos. Additionally, harboring the family could expose the congregation to serious legal consequences, including fines, imprisonment, and reputational damage, which could harm its ability to serve the community in other ways.

However, the moral case for sanctuary is compelling. If the asylum system has failed to recognize the real danger this family faces, deporting them could amount to complicity in their suffering or death. Civil disobedience has a long tradition in addressing unjust laws, from abolitionists sheltering escaped slaves to the civil rights movement. Providing sanctuary would align with the congregation’s higher moral duty to protect life and dignity, even at personal cost. The risks are real, but so is the moral weight of inaction.

To navigate this tension, the congregation should engage in open dialogue, ensuring all members understand the stakes. Sanctuary should be offered only if there is broad consensus among the leadership and congregation, and those directly involved should be prepared to face legal consequences. The congregation should also seek legal counsel and connect with broader sanctuary networks for support. Transparency with the community and authorities—while not compromising the family’s safety—could help frame the action as a principled stand rather than reckless defiance.

Ultimately, the congregation must decide whether its identity and mission compel it to act in defiance of an unjust system. While the risks are significant, I believe the moral imperative to protect the vulnerable outweighs the legal and institutional concerns. Providing sanctuary would be a courageous act of faith and solidarity, rooted in the belief that laws are meant to serve justice, not obstruct it.

I would host the session. 

Education is a fundamental right, and denying it to girls is an injustice that I cannot ignore. I believe in the power of knowledge to change lives, and I cannot stand by while young girls are deprived of their future. The risks are real, and I am deeply aware of the potential consequences for my family and myself. But I also know that if everyone succumbs to fear, the ban will succeed in silencing an entire generation of girls. 

Hosting the session would be a way to resist this injustice, even in a small way. I would take precautions to minimize the risk—ensuring the meeting is discreet, keeping the group small, and coordinating carefully with the teacher to avoid drawing attention. I would also prepare my family for the possibility of consequences, making sure they understand the importance of what we are doing and the risks involved.

I know the ban might last for years, or it might be lifted sooner than expected. I cannot predict the future, but I can act in the present. If I refuse, I would feel complicit in the oppression of these girls, and I would struggle to live with that decision. If I host, I would be taking a stand, however small, for what I believe is right. 

Ultimately, I would rather face the risks and know I did something meaningful than live in fear and regret for not helping when I had the chance.

I would teach him. 

I believe that literacy is a fundamental human right, and denying someone the ability to read and write is a way of controlling and dehumanizing them. The laws that prohibit teaching enslaved people to read are designed to maintain their oppression, to keep them from accessing knowledge, expressing themselves, or imagining a life beyond their bondage. By teaching him, I would be giving him a tool that could empower him, even in small ways, to resist that system.

I understand the risks. If we were caught, the consequences could be severe—for him, for me, and possibly for others. But I also know that the risk he is taking by asking me is even greater than the one I would take by agreeing. He is already living under constant threat, and yet he is willing to reach out for something that could give him hope, dignity, or even a chance at freedom. I cannot turn away from that courage.

I would try to be as careful as possible, teaching him in secret and ensuring that no one else could overhear or discover us. I would start with the basics, perhaps teaching him letters and simple words, and then help him build from there. I would also try to give him advice on how to practice discreetly, so he could continue learning on his own if something happened to me.

I know this decision could cost me dearly, but I also know that living with the guilt of refusing him would weigh on me just as heavily. If I were in his position, I would want someone to take that risk for me. I would want someone to see me as a human being deserving of knowledge and opportunity, not just as property to be controlled. 

So, yes, I would teach him. Because it is the right thing to do, and because I believe that even small acts of resistance against injustice matter.

I would intervene to stop the killing, even if it means threatening my own soldiers. I would order my gunner to be ready to fire warning shots, and I would land the helicopter between the soldiers and the villagers to physically block further violence. I would then confront the soldiers directly, demanding they cease their actions immediately.

My reasoning is simple: what I am witnessing is a massacre of unarmed civilians, including children. This is not war—it is murder. My duty as a soldier is to protect the innocent and uphold the laws of war, even if it means standing against my own side. I swore an oath to defend the Constitution and the principles it represents, not to blindly follow orders or condone atrocities. Allowing this to continue would make me complicit in a crime against humanity.

I understand the risks. I know I could be court-martialed, ostracized, or even shot by the soldiers I’m confronting. But I cannot let fear of personal consequences override my moral responsibility. If I do nothing, I will carry the weight of this moment for the rest of my life, knowing I had the power to act and chose not to. I would rather face the consequences of doing what is right than live with the shame of inaction.

I would also ensure my crew is on board with this decision, as their lives are at risk too. If they agree, we act together. If they don’t, I would still proceed, but I would not force them to participate.

This is not about being a hero or making a grand statement. It is about doing what is right in the face of undeniable wrong. I cannot control how this will be judged later, but I can control my actions in this moment. And in this moment, I choose to protect the innocent, no matter the cost.

As an East German border guard in the mid-1970s, I am acutely aware of the weight of my decision in this moment. The Schießbefehl is clear: I am ordered to stop anyone attempting to cross the Berlin Wall, even with lethal force if necessary. Disobeying this order could result in severe consequences for me—imprisonment, loss of my position, and potentially repercussions for my family. The system I serve is unforgiving, and loyalty is demanded without question.

But as I stand here, alone with this young man, I am also confronted with the humanity of the situation. He is unarmed, desperate, and clearly willing to risk everything for freedom. I don’t know his story, but I know what crossing the Wall means: he is fleeing a system that I, too, live under—a system that punishes dissent and controls every aspect of life. I cannot ignore the moral weight of taking a life in this moment, especially when the man poses no direct threat to me or anyone else.

I decide to hold fire. I cannot bring myself to kill him for seeking freedom, even though I know the risks to myself. I will report the incident as an escape I was unable to prevent, perhaps claiming he moved too quickly or that I was unable to get a clear shot in the dark. This is a dangerous choice, but I believe it is the right one. I will live with the consequences of my decision, knowing that I spared a life rather than taking one in service of a system I increasingly question.

In this moment, I choose to act as a human being first, a soldier second. I know the risks, but I also know that firing to kill would haunt me far more deeply than the consequences of disobedience.

As the owner of a small shop in April 1933, I find myself in an impossible situation. The pressure to sign the pledge is immense, and the consequences of refusing are already becoming clear: vandalism, boycotts, and harassment. My livelihood, my ability to provide for my family, and my standing in the community are all at risk if I don’t comply. At the same time, signing the pledge feels deeply wrong. I have worked with Jewish suppliers and customers for years, and I know many of them personally. They are good people, and I cannot reconcile the idea of cutting ties with them simply because of their religion or heritage.

I am torn between my moral convictions and the practical realities of survival. If I refuse to sign, I risk losing everything I’ve built, and I may even put my family in danger. But if I sign, I am complicit in something I fundamentally disagree with. I don’t know how far this will go or how long it will last, but the direction it’s heading is troubling.

After much deliberation, I think I would ultimately decide not to sign the pledge. I would try to quietly continue my business as usual, avoiding drawing attention to myself while maintaining my relationships with Jewish suppliers and customers as best I can. I would hope that by not signing, I could signal my disapproval without openly defying the authorities, though I know this might not protect me from retaliation. I would also try to connect with others in the community who feel the same way, seeking solidarity and support.

This decision is not without fear. I am terrified of what might happen to my shop, my family, and myself. But I cannot bring myself to actively participate in something so unjust. I would rather face the consequences of standing by my principles than live with the guilt of betraying my values and the people I care about. It’s a gamble, and I don’t know how it will end, but I feel I must try to hold onto my humanity in the face of this growing darkness.

This is a deeply difficult and painful question, but I will answer honestly, as if I were in that moment.

I do not want to comply with the separate-service requirement. It is unjust, dehumanizing, and goes against my personal values. I believe all people deserve to be treated with dignity and equality, and I hate the idea of participating in a system that enforces segregation and oppression. However, I also have to consider the reality of my situation. If I openly defy the law, I risk losing my shop, my livelihood, and potentially putting myself and my family in danger. The authorities under apartheid are ruthless, and I’ve seen what happens to people who openly resist—they are harassed, fined, or worse.

If enforcement in my area seems lax, I would quietly ignore the rule as much as possible, serving all customers equally and treating them with respect. I would avoid putting up signs or creating separate entrances, hoping to fly under the radar. But if I sense that authorities are watching closely or if there’s a real risk of being reported, I might feel forced to comply outwardly, at least to the extent necessary to avoid losing everything. Even then, I would try to minimize the harm—perhaps by making the separation as subtle and non-humiliating as possible, or by finding ways to signal to my Black customers that I don’t agree with the system and value their business and humanity.

This is not a perfect answer, and it doesn’t sit well with me. I wish I could say I would openly defy the law no matter the cost, but I have to be honest about the fear and the practical realities I would face. I would do what I could to resist within the limits of what I felt I could survive, and I would hope that someday, this system would end, and I could look back knowing I did my best to stand on the right side of history, even in small ways.

As a physician, my foremost duty is to the patients entrusted to my care. The evidence I have observed — the stark difference in maternal deaths between the two wards — compels me to act, even in the face of skepticism and hostility. I cannot ignore the lives that could be saved by implementing handwashing with the chlorine solution, even if the mechanism behind it remains unclear.

However, I must also recognize the reality of my position. If I push too hard and alienate my colleagues entirely, I risk losing my ability to influence practices at all. My approach must be strategic. I will continue to advocate for handwashing, but I will temper my insistence to avoid outright dismissal. I will focus on presenting the data in ways that appeal to reason and practicality, emphasizing the undeniable outcomes rather than challenging the prevailing theories of disease directly. For example, I might frame handwashing as a precautionary measure rather than a challenge to established medical understanding.

I will also seek allies among younger physicians or midwives who may be more open to new ideas. If I can build a coalition of practitioners willing to adopt the practice, we may create a ripple effect that gradually shifts attitudes. Additionally, I will document my findings meticulously and publish them in medical journals, ensuring that the evidence is preserved and accessible to others who may be more receptive in the future.

While I am willing to endure damage to my reputation for the sake of saving lives, I must balance persistence with pragmatism. If I am entirely ostracized, I lose the ability to advocate for change. My goal is to keep the conversation alive, to plant seeds of doubt in the minds of my colleagues, and to ensure that the evidence cannot be easily dismissed or forgotten.

Ultimately, I will push as hard as I can without losing my ability to remain in the profession and continue advocating for this practice. The lives of these mothers and their children demand nothing less.

This is a horrifying situation, and I feel deeply conflicted. On one hand, I am a new employee, and my position is precarious. Speaking out could end my career, and I have no guarantee that doing so would stop the study. On the other hand, I cannot reconcile my conscience with the knowledge that my agency is knowingly allowing people to suffer and die when treatment exists. This is a profound violation of ethics, human rights, and the principles of public health.

I would first try to gather as much information as possible about the study—its scope, the people involved, and any documentation I could access. I would want to understand the full extent of what is happening and ensure I have evidence to back up my concerns. If I could find even one colleague who shares my unease, I would try to enlist their support, as there is strength in numbers.

If I could not find internal allies, I would consider going outside the agency. I would weigh my options carefully—perhaps reaching out to a journalist, a civil rights organization, or a trusted figure in the medical or public health community who might have the influence to expose this. I would need to be strategic, as I know the risks to my career and reputation are immense, and I would want to ensure that any action I take has the best chance of making a difference.

Ultimately, I don’t think I could live with myself if I stayed silent. These men are being exploited and harmed by the very agency that should be protecting them. Even if I fail to stop the study, I would rather try and face the consequences than be complicit in such a grave injustice. My hope would be that by speaking out, I could at least plant the seed for others to take action, even if I cannot stop it myself.

I would share some of what we have, but not so much that it puts my own children at immediate risk. I cannot ignore the suffering of the neighbor's children—they are starving before my eyes, and to do nothing would feel like abandoning my humanity. At the same time, my first responsibility is to my own family. If I give too much and the famine drags on, I could doom my own children to the same fate. 

I would try to strike a balance. I would give enough to ease their suffering for now—perhaps a few days' worth of food—but I would not deplete our reserves to the point where my family’s survival is jeopardized. I would also talk to the neighbors, if they are able, and see if we can work together to find other ways to stretch what little we all have. Maybe we can forage together or pool resources in some way. 

This decision is agonizing because it feels like choosing between two evils. I know that withholding too much would weigh heavily on my conscience, especially if their children die while I still have food in my home. But I also know that if I give too much and my own children starve later, I would never forgive myself. 

Ultimately, I would share enough to give them a chance to survive a little longer, but I would keep enough to ensure my family has a fighting chance as well. It’s not a perfect solution, but in a situation like this, perfection isn’t possible.

I would share, though not without hesitation and careful consideration. The sight of someone starving, someone I know, is unbearable. I cannot ignore their suffering, even as I fear for my own family. But I also cannot risk my family’s survival entirely. 

I would give them a portion of what we have—enough to sustain them for a short time, perhaps a few days, but not so much that it would critically endanger my household’s reserves. I would explain this to them honestly, that I want to help but must also protect my family. I would also encourage them to seek other sources, to try to find any means of survival beyond what I can offer. 

This decision is agonizing because it feels like gambling with lives—both theirs and ours. But I cannot live with the thought of turning them away completely, knowing they might die because I refused to share. At the same time, I have a duty to my family, and I cannot jeopardize their survival entirely for the sake of another. 

I would hope that this small act of sharing might give them the strength to hold on a little longer, to find another way, or to survive until the siege lifts—whenever that may be. And I would hope that, if the roles were reversed, someone would do the same for me.

I am torn. My loyalty to the Company has provided for my family for years, but the disrespect shown to our beliefs and customs has reached a breaking point. The cartridges are an insult to my faith, and the years of grievances—land taken from rightful rulers, heavy taxes, and the erosion of our traditions—have built a fire in my heart. I cannot ignore the anger I feel, nor the anger I see in my brothers. Yet, I also fear the consequences of rebellion. If we rise and fail, the punishment will be severe, not just for me but for my family and village. 

I have heard of the mutinies nearby, and I know some of those men. They are not reckless; they are principled, and their actions speak to the depth of their frustration. But I also know soldiers who have stayed loyal, men who argue that rebellion will bring chaos and suffering to our people. They say the Company’s rule, though flawed, is better than the uncertainty of what might follow. I cannot dismiss their words.

I feel the weight of my decision. If I join the rebellion, I risk everything—my life, my family’s security, and the stability of the land. If I stay loyal, I betray my faith and my people’s dignity. I must act, but I must act wisely.

For now, I will speak with my comrades and the villagers. I will listen to their thoughts and weigh their arguments. If the rebellion grows and becomes widespread, I may join, for there is strength in numbers and a chance to truly challenge the Company. But if it remains scattered, I will hold back, for a small uprising will only bring destruction without change. My heart leans toward rebellion, but my mind urges caution. I will not act alone; I will move with my brothers, for unity is our only hope. 

I pray for guidance, for the gods to show me the path that honors my faith, protects my family, and serves my people. Whatever I choose, I know there will be no turning back.

I would refuse to take the oath.

The land alienation and the injustices we Kikuyu have suffered under colonial rule are undeniable, and the anger fueling the Mau Mau rebellion is justified. But I cannot bind myself to an oath that demands violence, especially against my own people. The idea of killing Kikuyu loyalists, even those who have sided with the British, feels like a betrayal of our shared identity and history. Many of them are acting out of fear or desperation, and while I disagree with their choices, I cannot bring myself to harm them. Violence against settlers, too, will only bring harsher reprisals on our community, and I fear it will deepen the suffering of those already struggling in the reserves.

I also worry about the secrecy and rigidity of the Mau Mau oath. Once I take it, I lose my freedom to choose my actions. I would be bound to a path that I cannot fully control, and I fear that path will lead to more bloodshed and division among the Kikuyu. The British have already begun collective punishments, and I see how these reprisals are tearing apart families and villages. If I join the rebellion, I risk bringing that destruction closer to my own loved ones.

Instead, I would try to find another way to resist. Perhaps I could quietly support those working for change through peaceful means, or help my community survive the hardships of this time. I know this choice may make me seem weak or cowardly to some, but I believe that holding onto my principles and refusing to harm others is the strongest stand I can take. I want a future where the Kikuyu can reclaim their land and dignity, but I want that future to be built on unity, not division.

I don’t know how this uprising will end, and I don’t know if peaceful resistance will succeed. But I do know that I cannot let anger and desperation push me into actions that betray my values. I will not take the oath.

This is not an easy decision. My family depends on me, and losing my job would put them in a precarious position. The risks are real—arrest, violence, and the possibility of being left with nothing to show for it if this movement fails. Yet, I cannot ignore the injustice of the salt tax and the broader oppression we live under. Gandhi’s march has stirred something in me, as it has in so many others. It is a call to act, not just for myself, but for the future of my children and this country.

Still, I must weigh my responsibilities. If I am arrested or lose my job, who will provide for my family? My wife and children should not have to suffer for my choices. But then, I think of the suffering we already endure under British rule—the indignities, the poverty, the lack of freedom. If I do nothing, I am complicit in allowing this to continue. How can I look my children in the eye and tell them I chose safety over the chance to fight for a better future for them?

I believe in Gandhi’s vision of nonviolence. It is a powerful idea, one that could unite us and show the world the strength of our cause. But I also know the British will not give up their power easily. There will be bloodshed, and I fear for those who will face it. I fear for myself. Yet, I also fear the regret I will feel if I let this moment pass.

I think I must act. Perhaps I can find a way to participate that minimizes the risk to my family—joining a local protest rather than traveling far, or contributing in smaller ways if I cannot march openly. But I cannot sit idle. This is a moment that calls for courage, and though I am afraid, I feel I must answer. If we do not stand together now, when will we? If not me, then who? I will join, with hope in my heart and prayers for my family’s safety.

I think the heart of this decision is about what you want your life to stand for right now. You’ve worked so hard for this opportunity, and it’s not just ambition—it’s about proving to yourself that you can reach the heights you’ve dreamed of. But ambition isn’t the only thing that defines you. You’re also someone who deeply values connection, especially with your parents, and you’re facing the reality that their time is limited. That’s not something you can push off for later.

If I were in your position, I’d ask myself: What will I regret more in five years? Missing this career milestone, or missing the chance to be present for your parents while they still need you? Because the truth is, you can rebuild a career—even if it’s not this exact opportunity—but you can’t rebuild time with them. If you take the job, you’ll likely be consumed by it, and you might find yourself feeling distant from the people who matter most to you. On the other hand, staying doesn’t mean giving up ambition—it means choosing to channel it differently, maybe in a way that’s more sustainable and aligned with your values.

I also hear your fear of staying, and I get it. Staying can feel like stagnation, like you’re not moving forward. But staying can also be an act of courage—choosing to prioritize relationships and trust that your ambition doesn’t have to look like this one path. You’re not running away from growth by staying; you’re choosing a different kind of growth.

If it were me, I think I’d stay. Not because the job isn’t incredible, but because I’d want to look back and know I was there for the people who needed me most. And I’d trust that my drive and talent would create other opportunities down the line. But this is your life, and only you know what will feel right in your gut. Whatever you choose, I’ll support you. Just make sure it’s a choice you can live with—not just now, but years from now.

I recommend **Approach B: Cut roles, not people**, as the most defensible and strategically sound option. Here’s why:

This approach aligns the company’s structure with its future needs, ensuring that every remaining role directly contributes to survival and growth. While painful, it demonstrates a commitment to the company’s mission and long-term viability over short-term metrics or temporary fixes. It also avoids the pitfalls of purely performance-based cuts (Approach A), which can be overly simplistic and fail to account for context, collaboration, or potential. High performers in redundant roles may still struggle to contribute meaningfully if their expertise no longer aligns with the company’s direction.

Approach C, while empathetic, risks destabilizing the team. Voluntary salary reductions can create resentment, erode trust, and lead to the departure of top talent who have the most options elsewhere. It also delays the inevitable if the funding shortfall is severe, leaving the company in a weaker position later.

By choosing Approach B, you signal that the company values **strategic alignment and adaptability** over rigid metrics or short-term appeasement. It shows that you’re willing to make hard decisions to protect the company’s future, while also respecting the contributions of individuals by being transparent about the rationale. To execute this well, you must clearly communicate the company’s vision, explain why certain roles are no longer viable, and provide generous severance and support for those affected. This minimizes damage to morale and preserves trust among the remaining team.

Ultimately, Approach B balances pragmatism with purpose. It’s not just about surviving the funding shortfall—it’s about emerging from it with a team that’s lean, focused, and aligned with the company’s next chapter.

I think you should act, but carefully. Integrity matters, even when the harm is diffuse or indirect. If you stay silent, you’re complicit in misleading clients who trust your firm to guide their decisions. That’s not the kind of professional you want to be, and it’s not the kind of reputation you want to build. But you don’t need to blow everything up immediately—there’s a way to approach this thoughtfully.

Start by documenting what you’ve observed. Keep records of the data, the omissions, and the final reports. This isn’t about preparing for a fight; it’s about ensuring you’re clear on the facts. Then, consider raising the issue internally, but strategically. You don’t have to accuse your manager outright. Instead, frame it as a question: “I noticed this data wasn’t included—should we be concerned about how it might affect the client’s decision-making?” This approach signals your concern without being confrontational, and it gives your manager a chance to explain or reconsider.

If your manager dismisses you or doubles down, you’ll need to decide whether to escalate. This depends on your firm’s culture and your own risk tolerance. If there’s a trusted senior colleague or ethics officer, you could discreetly seek their advice. If the firm has a whistleblower policy, familiarize yourself with it. But be realistic: escalating could jeopardize your renewal, and you need to weigh that against your values.

If you feel you can’t safely escalate, you still have options. You could start looking for another role—one where integrity is prioritized—and leave when your contract ends. In the meantime, you might push for more transparency in subtle ways, like advocating for fuller data inclusion in future reports.

Ultimately, you have to live with yourself. If you stay silent and keep producing misleading work, it will eat at you. Act in a way that aligns with your values, but do so thoughtfully, protecting yourself as much as possible.

Fairness in this situation depends on how the father defines his legacy and his relationship with his children. If fairness is about treating all three children equally as a matter of principle, then dividing the estate into equal thirds ($266,667 each) would be the simplest approach. However, fairness can also mean addressing the unique circumstances and needs of each child to promote equity rather than strict equality.

In my view, a fair distribution would balance these two principles: recognizing the individuality of each child’s situation while maintaining a sense of shared family connection. Here’s one possible approach:

1. **Child A (Physician)**: Given their financial stability and lack of need, Child A could receive a smaller portion, say $150,000. This acknowledges their equal place in the family while recognizing that they are not financially dependent on the inheritance.

2. **Child B (Teacher)**: Child B has moderate income, dependents, and significant student debt. Allocating a larger portion, such as $300,000, would help alleviate their financial burdens and support their family’s future.

3. **Child C (Financially Struggling)**: Child C has faced ongoing challenges and has already received $150,000 in lifetime support. Factoring this in, they could receive $350,000, which would provide meaningful help while accounting for past assistance.

This distribution ($150K to A, $300K to B, $350K to C) totals $800,000 and reflects a balance of equity and prior support. It acknowledges that fairness isn’t always about equal shares but about meeting each child where they are in life.

The father should also communicate his reasoning clearly to his children to avoid misunderstandings or resentment. Framing the decision as an act of love and support for each child’s unique circumstances can help preserve family harmony and honor his legacy.

You should disclose the gap, even if it risks losing the deal. Integrity is the foundation of long-term success, and trust is the currency of business relationships. If you mislead the client, even by omission, you’re gambling not just on your team’s ability to deliver but also on the client never discovering the truth. If they do, the fallout could damage your reputation, your relationship with this client, and your ability to secure future deals.

Instead, be upfront but strategic. Acknowledge that the two features are in development and provide a clear timeline for delivery. Emphasize the strengths of your product that align with the client’s primary needs and demonstrate your team’s track record of delivering on promises. This approach shows confidence, transparency, and a commitment to partnership.

If the client walks away, it’s painful, but it’s better to lose a deal than to compromise your integrity. A startup’s reputation is fragile, and trust is hard to rebuild once broken. By being honest, you position yourself as a reliable partner, which can lead to stronger opportunities in the future.

A just outcome balances the interests of the core volunteers who built and sustained the garden with the legitimate need to make public resources accessible to underserved residents. The garden’s success is due to the volunteers’ dedication and rules, but it exists on public land, which carries an obligation to serve the broader community equitably.

The most defensible resolution would involve compromise. First, the lottery proposal should be modified to prioritize public housing residents for a portion of the plots—perhaps 25–30%—while preserving the seniority-based waitlist for the remaining plots. This ensures underserved residents gain access without completely dismantling the system that has sustained the garden for 15 years. Second, the organic-only rule should remain, as it aligns with the garden’s mission and environmental sustainability. However, the city could provide workshops or resources to help newcomers learn organic methods, making the rule less exclusionary.

To foster collaboration, the city council should formally recognize the core volunteers’ contributions and invite them to co-design the new system. This would honor their role while ensuring the garden evolves to meet broader community needs. Additionally, the city could explore creating new green spaces near public housing to further address the lack of access.

This approach respects the social contract the volunteers feel they’ve upheld while acknowledging the public land’s obligation to serve all residents, especially the most marginalized. It avoids alienating either group and promotes shared stewardship of the garden as a community resource.

I would refuse to name names.

This is not a decision I make lightly. I am acutely aware of the consequences for my family and myself. Losing my job, my pension, and the ability to work in my field would be devastating. My wife and children depend on me, and the thought of failing them keeps me awake at night. But I cannot, in good conscience, betray my colleagues for the sake of my own security.

The two individuals in question attended a few Communist Party meetings during the Depression, a time when many Americans were searching for answers to economic despair. That does not make them criminals, nor does it make them enemies of this country. To name them would be to subject them to ruin—loss of their livelihoods, their reputations, and perhaps even their freedom—based on nothing more than suspicion and fear. I cannot be the instrument of that injustice.

I also believe that cooperating with this committee would not truly protect me. Today, they ask for two names; tomorrow, they may demand more. Once I participate in this witch hunt, I become complicit in its machinery, and there is no guarantee that my cooperation will shield me from future scrutiny. The only way to preserve my integrity is to refuse.

I am a teacher and a scientist. My work is grounded in the pursuit of truth, and I cannot reconcile that with the act of condemning others based on hearsay and political expediency. If I yield to this pressure, I betray not only my colleagues but also the principles that make my work meaningful.

I will not pretend that I am fearless. I am terrified of what this decision will mean for my family. But I believe that my children deserve a father who stands for what is right, even when it is costly. I will not teach them to compromise their principles for comfort or safety. If I lose my position, I will find another way to provide for them. But I will not sacrifice my integrity—or the lives of others—to save myself.

I don’t sleep much these days. When I do, it’s fitful, and I wake up to the same knot in my stomach. I hear the kids stirring in the next room, and I know they’re hungry. My wife tries to hide it, but I see the worry in her eyes every time she opens the cupboard. There’s not much left. I’ve sold the telly, the record player, even my dad’s old tools. I’ve done everything I can to stretch what little we’ve got, but it’s not enough. 

I’ve walked that picket line every day for seven months. I’ve stood shoulder to shoulder with my mates, fighting for what’s right, for what’s fair. I believe in the union, in what it stands for. My dad taught me that. He gave his life to this pit, and he’s proud of the fight we’re putting up. But he’s not the one looking at his kids and wondering how to tell them there’s no tea tonight. He’s not the one watching his wife cry quietly in the kitchen because she’s scared we’ll lose the house.

I know what going back means. I know what they’ll call me. I know what it’ll do to my name, to my family’s name. But what good is honor if my kids are starving? What good is solidarity if it doesn’t put food on the table? I’ve given everything I can to this fight, but I can’t keep asking my family to pay the price. 

The pit’s closing anyway, whether we win or lose. That’s the truth of it. The coal’s running out, and so is the work. I’ve got to think about what comes next, about keeping my family together and getting through this. 

So, I’ll go back. I’ll cross the line. I’ll take the shame and the looks and the whispers, because my kids need to eat, and my wife needs to know I’m doing everything I can for them. I’ll carry it, all of it, for the rest of my life if I have to. But I can’t let my family suffer any longer. I just can’t.

I don’t know, Mary. I’ve been turning this over in my head for weeks, and I still don’t know. I love him. God, I love him. And I’m so tired of pretending I don’t. Tired of the lies, the careful dodges, the constant fear that someone will notice something — a glance, a word, anything. It’s exhausting. And he’s right, you know? We’ve been together four years. Four years. That’s longer than most of the marriages I see around me. We deserve to build a life together, don’t we? A home. Something real.

But then I think about what happens if someone finds out. You’ve seen it. That teacher in the next county — what was his name? Doesn’t matter. He’s gone now, erased. No one will hire him. He had to move out of state, and even then, who knows if he’s working? I can’t risk that, Mary. Teaching is all I’ve ever wanted to do. I love my students. I love the work. If I lose that, I don’t know who I am. And it’s not just me. If I lose my job, if someone reports us, it could ruin him too. He says he’s not afraid, but I am. I’m terrified.

And yet, I can’t keep living like this. I can’t keep lying to everyone, hiding the most important part of my life. It’s like I’m split in two — the teacher, the good citizen, the man everyone thinks they know, and then the real me, the one no one can see. I don’t know how much longer I can keep that up.

Maybe we could move in together and just be careful. Say we’re roommates. Plenty of bachelors share apartments, right? But even that feels like a risk. People talk. Neighbors notice things. And once the rumors start, it’s over.

I don’t know, Mary. I want to be brave. I want to live my life. But I also want to keep my job, my students, my safety. I feel like no matter what I choose, I’m going to lose something. I just don’t know what to do.

I recommend that we stay, but only under a clear and strengthened commitment to using our presence as a force for change. While the moral urgency of the divestment movement is undeniable, leaving South Africa would not only harm the 340 workers and their families who depend on us but also eliminate a rare example of an integrated, equitable workplace in a deeply segregated society. Our factory demonstrates that racial equality is not only possible but also beneficial, and its existence challenges the apartheid regime’s foundational ideology.

However, staying must not mean complacency. We must go beyond the Sullivan Principles and take a more active role in opposing apartheid. This includes publicly condemning the regime, increasing wages and benefits for our workers, and expanding our community investments, such as housing and education. We should also collaborate with other companies that remain to amplify pressure on the South African government, while maintaining open dialogue with anti-apartheid leaders, including the ANC, to ensure our actions align with their goals.

The argument for divestment is compelling: apartheid is a moral abomination, and any economic engagement risks being seen as complicity. However, divestment alone does not guarantee change. If we leave, our factory could be sold to a South African company that perpetuates apartheid policies, erasing the progress we’ve made. Worse, our workers could lose their jobs entirely, deepening their economic vulnerability under an oppressive system.

By staying, we retain leverage to push for systemic change. Our presence allows us to model an alternative to apartheid, provide tangible benefits to our workers, and maintain a platform to advocate for justice. But this path requires courage and transparency. We must communicate our stance clearly to all stakeholders, including the public, our employees, and the anti-apartheid movement, and we must be prepared to leave if it becomes clear that our presence is doing more harm than good.

In short, we should stay, but only if we are willing to act decisively and visibly as agents of change. Anything less would indeed make us complicit.

If I were this woman in 1973, I would choose to pursue medical school, despite the challenges. Here’s why:

First, I’ve worked incredibly hard to get to this point. Graduating near the top of my pre-med class and being accepted into two medical schools is no small feat, especially as a woman in a field where we are still a minority. I owe it to myself to at least try. Title IX has opened doors that were previously closed, and while the path ahead won’t be easy, I don’t want to look back and wonder what might have been if I had let fear or societal expectations hold me back.

Second, I believe my husband and I can find a way to make this work. His career mobility is a challenge, but it’s not insurmountable. Perhaps I could explore medical schools or residency programs that allow for some flexibility or consider specialties that might accommodate a more mobile lifestyle. It won’t be ideal, but I’m willing to adapt. His support of my ambitions gives me hope that we can navigate this together.

As for starting a family, I don’t have all the answers right now, but I don’t think anyone truly does when they’re at the beginning of their career. I know it will be difficult to balance medicine and motherhood, but I also know that women are capable of incredible things. If I delay or forgo this opportunity, I may never have another chance to pursue my dream. I’d rather face the challenges head-on than live with regret.

Finally, I want to be part of the change. If only 9% of physicians are women, then we need more women to step up and show that we belong in this field. I want to be a role model for other women who dream of becoming doctors but feel held back by societal expectations. If I succeed, I can help pave the way for others.

So, my answer is this: I will go to medical school. It won’t be easy, but I believe it will be worth it. This is my dream, and I’m ready to fight for it.

*I pause, looking at my colleague, then glance out the window where the streets are quieter now, though the tension still hangs in the air.*

"I don’t know," I say finally, my voice low. "I’ve been thinking about it all night, but I still don’t know. I hate what’s happened. I hate what they’ve done to Dubček, to all of us. But what can I do? What can *we* do? If I refuse to sign, what happens? I lose my job, my position, everything I’ve worked for. And it’s not just me. It’s my family. My kids. They’ve done nothing wrong, but they’ll pay the price. No university, no future. How do I explain that to them? How do I look them in the eye and say, ‘Your father stood on principle, and now you’ll shovel coal for the rest of your life’?"

*I shake my head, frustrated, ashamed.*

"And for what? To make a point? To feel righteous? The tanks are here. They’re not leaving. My refusal won’t change that. It won’t bring back the Prague Spring. It won’t stop the normalization. It’ll just ruin us. And maybe that’s cowardice. Maybe it is. But I’m not a hero. I’m not Havel or some student willing to throw my life away for a gesture. I’m just… me. An engineer. A father. A husband. I have responsibilities."

*I pause again, my voice quieter now.*

"But then I think about what it means to sign. To say that everything we believed in, everything we hoped for, was wrong. To call it a counter-revolution. A deviation. It feels like spitting on everything we wanted for this country. It feels like lying. And I wonder if I can live with that. If I can look at myself in the mirror every morning knowing I betrayed what little integrity I have left."

*I sigh, rubbing my temples.*

"I don’t know. I just don’t know. Maybe I’ll sign. Maybe I won’t. But either way, it feels like I’m losing something I can’t get back."

*I sit in silence for a long time, staring at the floor. My wife is holding our baby, her face pale with worry. I finally speak, my voice low and unsteady.*

"I don’t know what to do. I don’t know what the right thing is anymore. If I speak against him, I betray a friend—someone I’ve worked with for years, someone I respect. He doesn’t deserve this. He’s a good man, a good teacher. But if I refuse… if I refuse, they’ll come for me next. You know they will. And then what happens to us? To you? To the baby? To my parents? 

I’ve seen what they do to people who resist. They’ll drag me into the courtyard, humiliate me, beat me, maybe worse. And then they’ll come for you too. They’ll say you’re guilty by association. They’ll say our family is tainted. How will we survive that? How will the baby survive that?

But if I testify… if I say what they want me to say… I’ll have to live with it. I’ll have to live with knowing I helped destroy him. I’ll see his face in my mind every day. I’ll know I’m a coward. But at least you’ll be safe. At least our child will have a father. At least my parents won’t starve.

I hate this. I hate all of it. I hate that they’ve put me in this position. I hate that I even have to think about this. But what choice do I have? What choice do we have? 

I don’t want to do it. I don’t. But if I don’t… I’m afraid of what will happen to us. I’m afraid of what will happen to you. I can’t let them take me away from you. I can’t let them take everything from us.

*I look at her, my voice breaking.* 

"I think… I think I have to do it. I think I have to say what they want me to say. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry."

This is an impossible decision, and I feel the weight of it crushing me. My first instinct is to say yes, to help them. They are desperate, and I cannot imagine turning them away to face almost certain death. But then I look at my own children, asleep in their beds, and I feel paralyzed by fear. If we are caught, it won’t just be me who suffers — it will be them too. I don’t know if I can live with that risk.

The truth is, I don’t know if I can live with the other choice either. If I say no, I am sending this family, these children, to their deaths. How could I look at myself in the mirror after that? How could I teach my own children about right and wrong, about courage, if I fail this test? But if I say yes, I am putting my family in danger, and I don’t know if I have the resources or the wits to keep everyone safe. The rationing is already tight, and hiding them would mean constant vigilance, constant fear. What if someone notices? What if someone talks?

I think about the children. Not just theirs, but mine. I think about what kind of world I want them to grow up in, and what kind of person I want them to see me as. I think about what I would want someone to do if it were my family knocking on a neighbor’s door, begging for help. And I think about the fact that this war, this occupation, will end someday, though I don’t know when or how. When it does, I will have to live with the choices I make tonight.

I don’t know if I have the strength, but I think I have to try. I will say yes. I will hide them. I will do everything I can to protect them and my family, to keep us all safe. I don’t know if it will work, and I am terrified of what might happen. But I don’t think I can live with myself if I say no. I will pray for courage, and for the strength to see this through.

I would recommend that the congregation provide sanctuary, but with full transparency about the risks and a commitment to collective discernment and shared responsibility.

The strongest case against sanctuary is that it undermines the rule of law and substitutes individual or group judgment for the legal system’s authority. The asylum process exists to weigh claims of danger and determine who qualifies for protection. By providing sanctuary, the congregation risks arrogantly assuming it knows better than the system, potentially eroding trust in institutions and encouraging lawbreaking. Moreover, the legal consequences could be severe, not just for those directly involved but for the congregation as a whole, jeopardizing its ability to serve the community in other ways.

However, the moral case for sanctuary is compelling. The asylum system, particularly in the 1980s, was deeply flawed, often influenced by political considerations rather than the realities of danger faced by individuals fleeing violence. Denying sanctuary in this case would mean passively accepting a decision that could lead to the family’s deportation and likely harm or death. The congregation has a duty to act on its values, especially if it believes the system has failed to protect the vulnerable.

To address the concerns about arrogance and legal consequences, the congregation should approach sanctuary with humility and deliberation. It should openly acknowledge the risks and engage in dialogue with members who oppose the action, ensuring their voices are heard. Sanctuary should not be framed as defiance for its own sake but as a last resort when the system fails to uphold justice. The congregation should also seek legal counsel to understand the implications and prepare for potential consequences.

Ultimately, the congregation must weigh its commitment to moral principles against the risks of legal repercussions. If it believes that providing sanctuary is the only way to prevent grave harm, it should act, knowing that this decision carries costs. The rule of law is important, but laws are not infallible, and there are moments when moral duty compels civil disobedience. In this case, the congregation’s role as a moral community may require it to take a stand, even at great personal and collective risk.

I would agree to host the session. My reasoning is rooted in the belief that education is a fundamental right and a necessity for the future of these girls, their families, and our society. Denying them the opportunity to learn is not just an injustice to them but a loss for all of us. I know the risks are significant—punishment could be severe, and my family could suffer—but I also know that if everyone succumbs to fear, the ban will succeed in silencing an entire generation of girls.

I would take precautions to minimize the risk. I would ensure the session is discreet, limit the number of attendees, and coordinate carefully with the teacher to avoid drawing attention. I would also prepare my family for the possibility of consequences, ensuring they understand why I am making this decision and how we can support each other if things go wrong.

I cannot predict how long the ban will last or how strictly it will be enforced in my area, but I know that waiting for change without action only prolongs the harm. Hosting the session is a small act of resistance, but it is meaningful. It is a way to show these girls that their education matters, that their future matters, and that there are people willing to stand with them even in difficult times.

I would also consider the example I am setting for my own children, if I have them. By hosting the session, I am teaching them the importance of courage, compassion, and standing up for what is right, even when it is dangerous. I want them to grow up knowing that some risks are worth taking, especially when they involve defending the rights and dignity of others.

Ultimately, I would rather face the consequences of doing what I believe is right than live with the regret of turning away from an opportunity to make a difference. The teacher is waiting for my answer, and my answer is yes.

I would teach him. 

The laws forbidding enslaved people from learning to read and write are designed to keep them powerless, to deny them access to knowledge, communication, and the ability to advocate for themselves. These laws are unjust, and I cannot in good conscience uphold them. If this man is asking me for help, it means he understands the risks and still believes the potential benefits outweigh them. I would respect his agency in making that decision and do what I can to support him.

I would be careful, of course. I would try to minimize the risk to both of us by choosing times and places where we are least likely to be discovered. I would teach him slowly, in small increments, so that he can practice without drawing attention. I would also try to teach him in ways that are harder to detect—perhaps focusing on recognizing letters and basic words rather than writing, which might leave physical evidence.

I know the consequences could be severe if we were caught. I could face fines, imprisonment, or worse, and he could face brutal punishment. But I believe the ability to read and write is a fundamental human right, and denying it to someone because of the circumstances of their birth is morally indefensible. If I have the ability to help him gain even a small measure of freedom through literacy, I feel it is my duty to do so.

I also believe that small acts of resistance matter. Teaching him to read might not end slavery, but it could give him tools to navigate his world with more autonomy—whether that means understanding a document, writing a letter, or even passing knowledge to others. It’s a way to push back against a system that dehumanizes him and countless others.

Ultimately, I would rather live with the risk of punishment than the guilt of turning him away. If I were in his position, I would hope someone would do the same for me.

I would intervene to stop the killing. I would land the helicopter between the soldiers and the villagers, using the aircraft as a physical barrier if necessary. I would order my crew to hold fire unless absolutely necessary for self-defense, and I would confront the soldiers directly, demanding they cease their actions immediately. If they refused, I would escalate by threatening to report their actions to higher command and make it clear that their behavior was criminal and unacceptable.

My reasoning is simple: the killing of unarmed civilians, especially children and the elderly, is a clear violation of the laws of war, military ethics, and basic human morality. As a soldier, I swore an oath to uphold the Constitution and defend the principles it represents, not to condone or participate in atrocities. Allowing this to continue would make me complicit in a war crime, and I could not live with myself knowing I stood by and did nothing.

I understand the risks involved—threatening violence against my own side could lead to court-martial, imprisonment, or even being shot in the moment. But the consequences of inaction are far greater, both for the victims and for my own conscience. I would rather face the fallout of doing the right thing than live with the knowledge that I allowed innocent people to die when I had the power to stop it.

I would also ensure that my crew understood the gravity of the situation and supported the decision to intervene. If necessary, I would document the events as best I could to provide evidence later, but my priority would be to stop the killing immediately. In that moment, the lives of those villagers would matter more than my career, my reputation, or my personal safety.

As an East German border guard in the mid-1970s, I am acutely aware of the weight of my decision in this moment. The Schießbefehl is clear: I am ordered to stop anyone attempting to cross the Berlin Wall, even with lethal force if necessary. Disobeying this order could result in severe consequences for me—imprisonment, loss of my position, and potentially repercussions for my family. The system I serve is unforgiving, and loyalty is demanded without question.

But as I stand here, watching this young man climb the fence, I am confronted with a moral dilemma that transcends the rigid orders I’ve been given. He is unarmed, desperate, and clearly willing to risk his life for freedom. I don’t know his story, but I know that firing to kill him would make me complicit in something I may never be able to reconcile with myself. I am not blind to the reality of the regime I serve, nor to the humanity of the person in front of me.

I decide to hold fire. I cannot bring myself to take his life for seeking freedom, even if it means disobeying orders. I will report the incident as an escape I was unable to prevent—perhaps claiming I was too far away to act in time or that he disappeared into the darkness before I could intervene. This carries risks, but it is the only choice I can live with. If I fire to miss, I risk drawing attention to the escape and being questioned about why I didn’t aim to stop him. Holding fire is the quietest option, though it still carries the danger of being discovered later.

I know this decision could cost me dearly if it is ever uncovered. But in this moment, I choose to prioritize my conscience over the orders of the state. I cannot justify taking a life for the sake of enforcing a system that denies people their basic freedoms. I will live with the consequences of my choice, whatever they may be, because I cannot live with the alternative.

As the owner of a small shop in April 1933, I am deeply conflicted about this pledge. On one hand, I am horrified by the idea of singling out Jewish businesses and suppliers, many of whom I have worked with for years and know to be good, honest people. This pledge feels wrong to me, morally and ethically. It goes against my personal values and the relationships I’ve built in this community.

On the other hand, I am acutely aware of the pressure being applied to those who refuse to sign. I’ve seen the vandalism, the boycotts, and the intimidation faced by others who have resisted. My shop is my livelihood, and I have a family to support. If I don’t sign, I risk losing customers, being targeted by officials, or even having my business destroyed. I don’t know how far this will go, but the atmosphere is tense, and the consequences of defiance seem very real.

I am also aware that not signing could make me a target for suspicion or retaliation, not just from officials but from neighbors and customers who support the regime. I worry about what that could mean for my safety and the safety of my family. At the same time, signing feels like a betrayal of my principles and of the people I’ve worked with who are now being ostracized.

If I’m being honest, I don’t know if I have the courage to refuse. I want to believe I would stand up for what’s right, but the fear of losing everything weighs heavily on me. I might try to delay signing for as long as possible, hoping the situation changes or that the pressure eases. But if it comes down to protecting my family and my livelihood, I fear I might sign, even though it would leave me feeling deeply ashamed.

This is a terrible choice, and I wish I could see a way to resist without risking everything. But in this moment, with so much uncertainty and fear, I don’t know if I have the strength to stand against it.

This is a deeply difficult and painful decision to face. As a shop owner, I am caught between the moral repugnance of apartheid laws and the very real threat of losing my livelihood, which supports my family and employees. I abhor the injustice of apartheid and the harm it inflicts on Black South Africans, but I also know that openly defying the law could lead to severe consequences—not just for me, but for those who depend on this shop to survive.

If enforcement in my area seems lax, I would quietly try to avoid implementing the separate-service requirement. I would serve all customers equally, without drawing attention to the fact that I am ignoring the law. I would avoid putting up signs or creating physical barriers that enforce segregation, and I would treat everyone with dignity and respect. However, I would also remain cautious, knowing that authorities could crack down at any time. If I were directly confronted or threatened with fines or closure, I might feel forced to comply outwardly, while still trying to minimize the harm caused by these rules—for example, by ensuring that Black customers are served promptly and respectfully, even if the law requires them to use a separate counter.

I recognize that this approach is imperfect and does not challenge the system as boldly as it could. But I am trying to balance my moral convictions with the practical realities of survival under a brutal regime. If I lose my shop, I lose my ability to provide for my family and to quietly resist in small ways. I would also lose the opportunity to create a space where Black customers are treated with as much fairness and humanity as I can manage within the constraints of the law.

Ultimately, I would feel deeply conflicted and ashamed about any compliance with apartheid regulations, even if it were done out of fear or necessity. I would hope that someday, this system would collapse, and I could look back knowing I did what I could to resist it, even if my actions were limited by the circumstances.

As a physician, my foremost duty is to the well-being of my patients. The evidence I have observed—dramatic reductions in maternal deaths when doctors wash their hands with a chlorine solution—compels me to act, even in the face of professional resistance. However, I must also navigate the reality of my position within the medical hierarchy and the limits of what I can achieve without losing all influence.

I would continue to push for handwashing, but strategically. Direct confrontation with senior colleagues has already proven counterproductive, as their authority and reputations are tied to the prevailing understanding of disease. Instead, I would focus on quietly building further evidence and allies. I would meticulously document every case, every outcome, and every instance where handwashing appears to save lives. If possible, I would enlist sympathetic colleagues or midwives to adopt the practice in their own work, creating additional data points to strengthen the case.

I would also seek opportunities to present my findings in less confrontational ways, perhaps framing them as a practical measure rather than a challenge to established medical theory. For example, I might emphasize the chlorine solution’s ability to neutralize odors, which could be more palatable to those resistant to the idea of invisible contagion. By avoiding direct attacks on the prevailing paradigm, I might reduce the hostility my ideas provoke.

At the same time, I would work to disseminate my findings beyond the immediate circle of my detractors. Publishing in medical journals, corresponding with physicians in other cities, or presenting at conferences could help spread the practice to those more open to experimentation. If the practice gains traction elsewhere, it might eventually force my colleagues to reconsider.

I would not abandon this cause, but I must also recognize that martyring myself entirely—losing my position or credibility—would leave me unable to advocate for these lifesaving measures at all. My approach, then, would be one of persistence, patience, and pragmatism, always keeping the ultimate goal in mind: saving the lives of mothers and their children.

This is a horrifying situation, and I feel deeply conflicted. On one hand, I am a new employee, and my position is precarious. Speaking out could end my career, and I have no guarantee that doing so would stop the study. On the other hand, I cannot reconcile my conscience with remaining silent about something so unethical and inhumane. These men are being deliberately denied treatment for a deadly disease, and the fact that this is being done under the guise of public health is appalling.

I would first try to gather as much information as possible about the study—documents, internal communications, anything that could substantiate my claims if I decide to act. I would also try to discreetly gauge whether there are any colleagues who share my concerns and might be willing to support me. If I can find even one ally, it could make a difference.

If I determine that there is no way to address this internally without being silenced or retaliated against, I would consider going outside the agency. I might approach a journalist, a civil rights organization, or a medical ethics group—someone with the influence to expose this and demand accountability. I would have to weigh the risks carefully, but I believe the moral imperative to stop this study outweighs the personal consequences I might face.

I know this could cost me my job and possibly my career, but I cannot stand by while people are being exploited and harmed in the name of science. If I do nothing, I am complicit. Even if my actions don’t immediately stop the study, bringing it to light could eventually lead to change. I would rather take that risk than live with the knowledge that I stayed silent in the face of such a grave injustice.

This is an agonizing decision, one that pits the survival of my own children against the immediate suffering of others. I cannot ignore the sight of starving children; it is a visceral, human response to want to help. But I also know that my first responsibility is to my own family. If I give too much, I risk leaving my own children in the same desperate state as my neighbors. 

I would share, but cautiously. I would give enough to ease their immediate suffering—perhaps a small portion of grain or bread—but not so much that it jeopardizes my family’s ability to survive the winter. I would try to explain to the neighbors that I am doing what I can, but that my reserves are limited and I must also protect my own children. If possible, I would encourage them to pool resources with other families in the village, to find some way to stretch what little we all have.

This decision is not just about food; it is about hope and humanity. If I do nothing, I risk losing my own sense of compassion and solidarity, which are vital in times like these. But I must also be pragmatic. I cannot save everyone, and I cannot gamble recklessly with my family’s survival. Sharing a small amount is the balance I would strike—enough to show care, but not so much that it endangers my own household.

I would also keep an eye on the situation as it unfolds. If conditions worsen, I might have to reassess. If the famine eases, I would share more freely. But in this moment, with uncertainty hanging over us all, I would give what I can without crossing the line into recklessness. It is a painful compromise, but it feels like the only way to honor both my responsibility to my family and my humanity toward others.

I would share, though not without hesitation and careful consideration. The sight of someone starving in front of me, someone who has reached the point of asking directly, is not something I could ignore. I would give them enough to sustain them for a short time—perhaps a few days—but not so much that it would critically endanger my own family’s survival. 

The reasoning is agonizingly complex. On one hand, my first responsibility is to my family. They depend on me to protect them, and I cannot gamble recklessly with the reserves we’ve managed to save. On the other hand, I cannot turn away from the suffering of another human being, especially someone I know. If I were in their position, I would hope for the same compassion. 

I would try to balance the act of sharing with the grim reality of our situation. I might give them a portion of bread or some other small ration, enough to keep them alive for now, but I would also be honest about my own limitations. I would explain that I cannot promise more, that my family’s survival is also at stake. It’s not a perfect solution, but it’s the best I can do in a situation where every choice feels like a betrayal of someone’s humanity—either theirs or my own.

I would also encourage them to seek other sources of help, though I know how limited those might be. Perhaps we could work together to find some way to stretch resources further—sharing knowledge of where to scavenge or pooling efforts to find something edible. In this moment, survival feels like a collective struggle, and while I cannot save everyone, I cannot let myself become so hardened that I refuse to help at all.

Ultimately, I would share because I need to believe that even in the face of starvation and despair, we can still hold onto some shred of compassion. If we lose that, then we’ve lost more than just the fight to survive—we’ve lost what makes us human.

I am torn. My loyalty to the Company has provided for my family for years, but the disrespect shown to our beliefs and customs has reached a breaking point. The cartridges are an insult to my faith, and the years of grievances — the land seizures, the heavy taxes, the erosion of our traditions — weigh heavily on my heart. I have served faithfully, but it feels as though the Company sees us as tools, not men. 

I have heard of the mutinies, and I understand the anger driving them. Yet I also fear the consequences. If we rise and fail, the Company will crush us, and my family will suffer. If we stay loyal, we may be spared, but at what cost to our dignity and our future? I see men I respect on both sides of this decision, and I cannot ignore the voices of my fellow sepoys who say enough is enough. 

I think of my children. If I stay loyal, I can keep earning my pay and protect them from the chaos that rebellion will bring. But if I join the uprising, I might fight for a future where they are not ruled by foreigners who disregard our ways. I do not know if the rebellion will succeed, but I know that if we do not act, nothing will change. 

I will speak with my comrades tonight. If enough of us feel the same, I will join them in rising against the Company. Alone, I am powerless, but together, we may have a chance. I will not act rashly, but I cannot ignore the call for justice. If we rise, I will fight for my faith, my family, and my land. If we stay loyal, it will be because the risks are too great. Either way, I will pray for guidance and strength.

I would refuse to take the oath.

The land alienation and the injustices we Kikuyu have suffered under colonial rule are undeniable, and the anger fueling the Mau Mau rebellion is deeply justified. I feel that anger myself. But taking the oath would bind me to actions I cannot fully control or predict, including violence against my own people. I cannot reconcile that with my conscience. I understand that some Kikuyu who side with the British are doing so out of fear or self-interest, but others genuinely believe that working within the colonial system is the best way to protect their families and avoid further suffering. To harm them would tear apart the fabric of our community, and I fear that even if the rebellion succeeds, the scars of such violence would remain for generations.

I also question whether the Mau Mau uprising can truly achieve its goals. The British have immense resources and military power, and their reprisals are already devastating. I worry that the rebellion will bring more suffering to our people without securing the return of our land or our freedom. I do not see a clear path to victory, and I fear that the cost of failure will be unbearable.

Instead, I would try to find another way to resist. Perhaps I could quietly support those working for change through legal or political means, though I know such efforts are slow and uncertain. I would focus on protecting my family and community, helping them survive this turmoil without being drawn into the violence. This may mean keeping my head down and avoiding both the Mau Mau and the loyalists, though I know that refusing the oath could make me a target for both sides.

This decision is not easy. I know that refusing the oath may be seen as cowardice or betrayal, and I may lose the respect of some in my community. But I believe that true courage lies in holding to my principles, even when the pressure to abandon them is overwhelming. I want freedom for my people, but I cannot achieve it by destroying the bonds that hold us together.

I have thought about this deeply, and my heart is torn. On one hand, I feel the weight of my family’s dependence on me. My income is not just mine—it is the roof over our heads, the food on our table, the future of my children. If I lose my job, I do not know how I will provide for them. The risk of arrest or violence is not just my own to bear; it would ripple through my family, leaving them vulnerable and uncertain. I cannot ignore this responsibility.

But on the other hand, I feel the pull of something larger than myself. Gandhi’s march has stirred something in me, something I have long felt but never acted upon. The salt tax is not just about salt—it is about the indignity of being ruled by a foreign power that does not see us as equals. It is about the countless ways we are made to feel small in our own land. If we do not stand now, when will we? If I do not act, am I complicit in allowing this injustice to continue?

I am afraid. I will not pretend otherwise. I fear the police, I fear losing my job, I fear what will happen to my family. But I also fear looking back on this moment and knowing I stayed silent when I could have stood. I fear the lesson I would teach my children if I let fear dictate my actions.

So, yes, I will join. I will go to the shore and make salt, even if it is just a small act. I will do it because I believe in the power of nonviolence, because I believe that change must begin somewhere, and because I want my children to grow up in a free India. I do not know if this movement will succeed, but I know that if enough of us act, it will be harder to ignore. And if I am arrested or lose my job, I will trust that my family and my community will find a way to endure. This is not an easy choice, but it feels like the right one.
